Read this:

I'm Tara, and my desk faces the small meeting corner where Ishita meets Dilnaz on Wednesdays. Last week Dilnaz arrived stuck on a slow report page. I expected Ishita to type the fix. Instead Ishita asked, 'What have you tried?' Dilnaz listed two things. 'What else could it be?' Dilnaz named three options, hesitating. 'And if you chose the second one, how might it go wrong?' Dilnaz went quiet, then said, 'It could hide the real problem.' Ishita nodded and asked which option to test first. Twenty minutes later Dilnaz was typing alone. I can't say whether it felt frustrating or exciting to Dilnaz, but Dilnaz left with the answer and a small grin.

How many options did Dilnaz name?
Dilnaz named three options.
What might Dilnaz have been feeling when going quiet?
Dilnaz was possibly uncertain and concentrating hard, and the small grin at the end suggests some satisfaction.
What could Ishita do if Dilnaz stayed stuck?
Ishita could give a small hint about where to look, without solving it, since a nudge keeps the thinking with Dilnaz.
How might Tara have seen Ishita's way of helping?
Tara expected a typed fix, so was probably surprised and interested in how much Dilnaz did alone.

Read this:

Monday. Pooja arrives at Arohi's desk with a failing test. 'Just tell me what's wrong.' Arohi pulls up a chair but keeps her hands in her lap. 'What have you tried so far?' Pooja lists two things. 'What else could it be?' Pooja guesses three more. 'How would each one fail?' Forty minutes later, Pooja finds it herself: a time-zone bug.
Thursday. Another problem, a slow page. Pooja writes on a notepad before coming over: what I tried, three options, how each might fail. Arohi asks only one question. Pooja goes back and fixes it.
The next Wednesday. Pooja doesn't come to Arohi's desk at all. Instead she messages: 'Found a memory leak. Tried two things, the third one worked. Wrote it up for the team.' Arohi reads it twice and smiles.

What bug did Pooja find on Monday?
A time-zone bug.
What does Arohi's smile on Wednesday suggest?
It suggests Arohi feels proud and pleased that Pooja can now reason through problems alone.
Why did Arohi keep her hands in her lap on Monday?
To make Pooja think through the options instead of watching a fix, so the reasoning becomes Pooja's own.
How did Pooja's experience change over the week?
Pooja moved from wanting an answer to arriving with options, and finally solved a problem alone and shared it with the team.

messages.content:
Read this:

Nikita, you asked how to mentor your first junior. Let your Aadhya Didi tell you about mine. I was twenty-four, stuck on a database migration, and I went to Mr Menon expecting an answer. He gave me three questions instead. What have you tried? What are all the options? How might each one fail? I was annoyed. I wanted him to just tell me. But I answered, and halfway through the third question, I saw my own mistake: I'd planned to migrate everything at once, and it would have locked the system for hours. He hadn't said a word about it. Twenty years later, I still ask myself those three questions before every big change. So when your junior comes to you, don't hand over the solution. Hand over the questions.

What three questions did Mr Menon ask?
What have you tried? What are all the options? How might each one fail?
How did Aadhya feel when Mr Menon gave questions instead of an answer?
She was annoyed at first, wanting a quick answer, before discovering her own mistake.
What was the turning point in Aadhya's story?
Answering the third question and spotting, without being told, that migrating everything at once would lock the system.
How might Mr Menon have seen that conversation?
He likely felt quietly satisfied seeing Aadhya find the mistake herself, which is why he said nothing about it.

Read this:

I'm Sahil. When Rehana admitted she had pushed a change without testing and broken the build, I could see her bracing. So I told her about the worst project of my early career: a billing module I insisted on rewriting alone, then hid my delays for weeks, and shipped late with bugs that cost a client an evening of manual work. I kept it to three minutes, no dramatic ending, because this wasn't my moment. What I learned, I said, was that telling the team early would have saved everyone time. Then I turned it back to her: 'What would you want the team to know about yesterday?' Rehana let out a breath and began to explain. Later she said it was easier to talk once she knew I had stumbled too.

How long did Sahil's story take?
Sahil kept it to three minutes.
What did Sahil want to make sure of while telling the story?
Sahil was concerned that Rehana was bracing herself, so Sahil kept the story short and turned it back to her, making sure the talk stayed about her.
What could Sahil do if Rehana still stayed quiet about the mistake?
Sahil could offer to go through the change together on a shared screen, since working side by side takes away some of the pressure of explaining.
How did the story feel to Rehana?
Rehana felt relieved and safer: she let out a breath, and later said it was easier to talk knowing Sahil had stumbled too. 🙂

Read this:

Mentoring programme observation note, session 4.
I sat in on Trisha's session with her mentee, Chetan, today. For three sessions Chetan had said everything was 'fine', though his project was clearly behind. Today Trisha tried something different. She told him about her first year: a dashboard project she had promised in six weeks that took five months, and how she hid the delay until her manager heard about it from a client. She kept it to about four minutes, then turned it back to him: 'So, how's yours really going?'
Chetan was quiet, then admitted he was two weeks behind and scared to say so. They spent the rest of the hour on a plan to tell his lead.
Trisha stopped her story before it became about her, which mattered. I have suggested she keep that balance.
Programme coordinator

How long did Trisha's dashboard project actually take?
Five months, instead of six weeks.
What was Chetan feeling before he admitted the delay?
Chetan was scared to admit being two weeks behind, which is why everything had been 'fine' for three sessions.
Why did Trisha keep the story to about four minutes?
So the session stayed about Chetan; a short story made it safe to admit mistakes without turning the focus to Trisha.
How might Chetan's lead be affected by the plan?
The lead will hear about the delay early from Chetan, which gives time to adjust instead of a surprise later.

Read this:

Thursday, 10 p.m.
Tonight I told Chinmay about the worst launch of my life: the app I released on a Friday that logged out every user in the country. I told it in five minutes, with the embarrassing bits: I cried in the parking lot, I nearly quit. Then I stopped, because I noticed I was starting to enjoy telling it.
I asked him about his week. And for the first time in two months, he didn't say 'all good'. He said he'd merged something without tests and was terrified it would break. We opened it together and added the tests.
Note to self: the story is a door, not a stage. Walk him through it, then get out of the way.
Sarita

What did Sarita's app do when it was released on a Friday?
It logged out every user in the country.
Why did Sarita stop telling the story, and how did Sarita feel about it?
Sarita felt a little uneasy on noticing a growing enjoyment in telling it, and did not want the session to become about the mentor.
What does Sarita mean by 'the story is a door, not a stage'?
Sharing a failure should open space for the mentee to speak, not become a performance about the mentor.
How might Chinmay see Sarita after hearing the story?
Chinmay may see Sarita as human and safe to be honest with, since Sarita admitted crying and nearly quitting.

Yash: Bhai, how do I apply for a master's abroad? Deadlines are close.
Kishore: Easy. Do your exam first, then send applications at the end of the month. Universities don't mind late ones.
Yash: Really? Nothing needed before that?
Kishore: Trust me, everyone does it that way 👍
[three weeks later]
Yash: Kishore, two universities say their deadline was last week 😟
Yash: I waited like you said
Kishore: Oh no. I've never actually applied abroad. I assumed it works like our college admissions. I should have said I don't know.
Yash: Now I've probably lost a year
Kishore: Let's find someone who has done it. The universities' international offices can give exact dates too. I'm sorry.
Yash: ok. Thanks for saying it.

When did Yash learn that two universities had passed their deadlines?
Yash learned it three weeks later.
How did Kishore feel after Yash's message about the deadlines?
Kishore felt regretful and ashamed, admitting to never having applied abroad and to having assumed it worked like college admissions.
What could Kishore have done when Yash first asked?
Kishore could have said honestly that Kishore did not know the process and pointed Yash to an international office or someone who had applied.
How might Yash be feeling about the lost year?
Yash is probably worried and disappointed, though thanking Kishore for the honesty suggests some trust remains.

Read this:

In the small town of Hosapete, Rajni was the person young people asked for advice. She had a good job in Bengaluru and came home every month. When Madhuri, a final-year engineering student, asked about a master's in Germany, Rajni answered at once. 'Apply in March, like here. Transcripts can come later.'
She had never applied abroad. She didn't say so.
Madhuri planned around March. In February she opened the university's page for the first time: the deadline for her course had been 15 January, and her documents needed a certification that took six weeks. She had missed the year.
When Madhuri told her, Rajni sat quietly on the bus stand bench. 'I should have said I didn't know,' she said at last. 'And sent you to someone who did.'

When had the deadline for Madhuri's course been?
15 January.
How did Rajni feel on the bus stand bench?
Rajni felt ashamed and regretful, knowing her confident guess cost Madhuri a year.
What should Rajni have said when Madhuri asked?
That she didn't know the process abroad, pointing Madhuri to the university's official page or someone who had applied.
How was Madhuri affected by the advice?
Madhuri trusted it, planned around the wrong month and missed the year, likely feeling disappointed and let down.

Read this:

In a small Accra office after work, Kofi was known as the mentor who always had an answer. When Yosef, a junior analyst he mentored, mentioned a master's in Canada, Kofi leaned back confidently. 'Easy. Apply in spring, get the study permit after you're accepted, it takes a few weeks.' Kofi had studied locally and never applied abroad, but he didn't want to look unsure.
Yosef followed the plan. He was accepted in May, then learnt from the official immigration page that permit processing from Ghana could take months and required proof of funds he hadn't prepared. His September start slipped to January, and he lost his deposit.
Over coffee, Kofi rubbed his forehead. 'I should have just said, "I don't know, let's find someone who does."'

What did Yosef lose when his start slipped?
His deposit.
Why didn't Kofi admit he had never applied abroad?
Kofi didn't want to look unsure, proud of being the mentor who always had an answer.
What could Kofi have done instead?
Said he didn't know and connected Yosef with someone who had studied in Canada, or pointed to the official immigration page.
How might Yosef feel about Kofi's advice now?
Yosef may feel frustrated and let down, having lost his deposit and a term by trusting a confident guess.

Read this:

I'm Zoya, and I share a desk with Dhruv, so I hear his mentoring calls. On Thursday Maria asked about switching into data journalism, and Dhruv said, 'That's outside what I know, I'd only be guessing.' I noticed he didn't leave it there. He picked up his phone, messaged a friend who works at a news desk, and wrote, 'My mentee Maria is thinking about your line of work. Could you give her twenty minutes?' Then he told Maria the friend's name and said he'd check in after the chat. Maria looked surprised, maybe a little nervous, and copied the name into her notes. A week later Maria mentioned that the friend had also introduced her to a reporter who ran a small open data project.

What did Dhruv say when Maria asked about data journalism?
Dhruv said, 'That's outside what I know, I'd only be guessing.'
What might Maria have been feeling when Dhruv passed on the friend's name?
Maria seemed surprised and maybe a little nervous, as Zoya notes, though Maria may also have felt grateful.
What could Dhruv add to help Maria use the twenty minutes well?
Dhruv could ask Maria to prepare two questions beforehand, so the short chat with the friend is spent on what matters most to her.
How might Dhruv's friend at the news desk see the request?
The friend probably sees a colleague who trusts them and may be glad to help, since twenty minutes is a modest ask.

Monday. At their weekly chat, Noor asks Suraj how to move from testing into UX design. Suraj thinks, then says honestly, 'That's not my field. I'd be guessing. But I know someone who knows.'
Wednesday. Suraj sends a short message to his friend Pallavi, a UX designer at another company: 'My mentee Noor is exploring UX. Would you have twenty minutes for a call? No pressure.' Pallavi says yes. Suraj introduces them in one email with a line about each.
Two Saturdays later. Noor reports back at their chat, bright-eyed. Pallavi reviewed her sample case study, suggested an online course and invited her to a local design meetup. 'I met five designers there,' Noor says. Suraj grins. 'Now you've got more mentors than I have.'

What did Pallavi suggest after reviewing the case study?
An online course, plus an invitation to a local design meetup.
How did Noor feel when reporting back?
Noor was excited and encouraged, bright-eyed after meeting five designers.
Why was Suraj's honesty about UX a good choice?
Admitting it wasn't his field let him connect Noor with someone who knew, instead of giving guesses.
How might Pallavi see being introduced?
Pallavi got a clear, low-pressure request and may enjoy helping someone keen to enter the field.

Keerthana, you asked how I ended up in climate data when I trained as a web developer. Your Divyansh sir will tell you. At twenty-four, I asked my mentor, Mrs Rao, about working on climate projects. She could have made something up. Instead she said, 'I know nothing about that world. But my college friend at the weather institute does.' That same evening she emailed him: two lines about me, two about why she thought we should talk. He met me for tea the next week. He introduced me to two researchers, one of whom later hired me. Mrs Rao never taught me a single thing about climate. What she gave me was a door to the right people. So when your mentee asks something outside your field, don't guess. Open a door.

Where did Mrs Rao's college friend work?
At the weather institute.
How might Divyansh have felt when Mrs Rao said she knew nothing about that world?
He may have felt surprised, even disappointed for a moment, then grateful when she made the connection that same evening.
What was the turning point in Divyansh's story?
Mrs Rao emailing her friend at the weather institute that evening, which led to tea, two researchers and a job.
How might Mrs Rao's friend have seen the introduction?
He got a short, clear email from a trusted friend, which made it easy and pleasant to agree to meet.

I'm Joseph, and I mentored Rajni for a year. Rajni was the first in the family to finish college, and in our early meetings I'd ask, 'Any questions?' and get, 'No, sir, all clear.' Then Rajni's work would come back with the same doubts, unasked. Around the fourth session I noticed the pattern and realised my plan, with questions put on the spot, suited me and not Rajni. So I changed. I began sending a short note two days before each meeting with the topics, and Rajni wrote questions back on paper. In the room I left a few quiet minutes with nothing to say. The first question that came out of that silence was a real one, about how to ask for feedback. Others kept coming.

Around which session did Joseph notice the pattern?
Joseph noticed it around the fourth session.
What was Joseph feeling when the same doubts came back unasked?
Joseph was puzzled and concerned that the mentoring was not reaching Rajni, which led Joseph to rethink the plan.
What other change could Joseph try for Rajni?
Joseph could ask how Rajni likes to learn and open a message channel for questions between meetings, since some people find asking in writing easier.
How might Rajni have felt in the quiet minutes?
Rajni probably felt less pressed, having time to think, since the first real question came out of that silence.

Read this:

I'm Ankita, and I sat near Vishal the year he mentored Sagar, a first-generation graduate who had joined from a small-town college. In their first meetings, Vishal did most of the talking and kept asking, 'Any questions?' Sagar always said no, and then I'd see him searching the same topic online for an hour afterwards. After the third meeting Vishal changed things. He started sending Sagar a short written note two days before each meeting: what they'd cover, and three questions Sagar could think about. In the meetings, he'd ask something and then just wait, sometimes for a long while, without filling the silence. By the second month, Sagar was bringing written questions of his own. I don't know what Vishal was thinking when he changed his style. But he stopped saying 'Any questions?'

What did Vishal send Sagar two days before each meeting?
A short written note of what they'd cover and three questions to think about.
What might Sagar have been feeling in the first meetings?
Sagar was probably shy and hesitant, worried about looking unprepared, so he said no and searched alone later.
Why did the written notes and silences work better than 'Any questions?'
They gave Sagar time to prepare and space to speak, suiting his style instead of expecting instant questions.
How does Ankita see Vishal's change?
Ankita notices a mentor who adjusted to the person, and sees it working as Sagar starts bringing questions.

Week one. Chetan meets Ishita, his new mentee, a first-generation graduate from a village near Sangli. He talks for forty minutes about system design. She nods and says, 'Clear, sir.' Later, her lead tells him she's struggling with the basics.
Week three. Chetan notices she never asks anything in front of others. So he changes the plan. Two days before each meeting, he sends her a short note: the topic, a small example, and 'write down anything unclear, however small'. In meetings he asks a question and waits, counting silently to ten.
Week eight. Ishita arrives with a page of questions in her neat handwriting, the first one starting 'This might be silly, but'. None of them are silly. Chetan answers each one. At the end she asks, 'Can we do this again Thursday?'

What did Ishita say in week one?
'Clear, sir.'
What does 'This might be silly, but' suggest Ishita still feels?
It suggests Ishita still feels a little shy and unsure, but now safe enough to ask.
What else could Chetan do to keep adapting?
He could ask Ishita which format helps most, notes, examples or calls, and keep adjusting as her confidence grows.
How might Ishita's lead see the change by week eight?
The lead would likely see her basics improving and more willingness to ask, easing the worry from week one.

Sunday night. A third person asked me to mentor them this week, and I said no. It was awkward. Last spring I had four mentees plus the release crunch, and I cancelled on two of them; one went quiet and I'm not sure I ever fixed that. So the rule now: two at a time, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, forty-five minutes, and I say so upfront. Hemant is one of my two, and I'd rather give Hemant a reliable slot than a maybe. Wrote to the third person offering to recommend a colleague and a date when I might have space. Felt guilty for an hour, then fine. Sessions kept beat sessions promised. — Tejas

How many mentees does Tejas take at a time?
Tejas takes two mentees at a time.
How did Tejas feel after saying no to the third request?
Tejas felt guilty for an hour and then fine, having protected the sessions already promised.
What other approach could Tejas use for people who ask but cannot fit in?
Tejas could run a group session once a month for those people, which shares some help without a weekly promise.
How might Hemant see the arrangement?
Hemant probably feels secure that sessions will happen, having a reliable slot instead of a maybe.

Jeevan: hi Noor! my friend said you mentor people. could you take me on? 🙂
Noor: hi Jeevan, thanks for asking. honestly, I only mentor two people at once, and I have two right now
Jeevan: oh. even just once a month?
Noor: I tried three last year. I ended up cancelling on all of them in the busy months. that felt worse than saying no
Noor: my two finish in March. I can put you first on the list for April if you like
Jeevan: yes please
Noor: meanwhile I can send you two good resources, and I'm free for one 20-min call this Saturday to point you in the right direction. that one I can promise
Jeevan: that's really kind. Saturday works
Noor: great. I'll send an invite. and in April we start properly 👍

In March.
How did Noor feel about taking three mentees last year?
Noor felt bad, even guilty, about cancelling on all of them in the busy months.

It helps Jeevan now without overcommitting, and it's a promise Noor can actually keep.

In Nanded, word had spread that Nandini, who worked at the bank and had cleared a tough engineering entrance herself, mentored students on Sundays. By June, six parents had asked. Disha, whose daughter was in Class 11, came to the house with a box of pedas and a hopeful face.
Nandini made tea and thought it through before answering. Last year she had said yes to five students and ended up cancelling half the Sundays and rushing the rest. 'Two is what I can do well,' she said. 'I have two now, until December.' She wrote her Sunday hours on a slip of paper: 10 to 12, only those. 'I can take your daughter from January. Until then, she can come to the free doubt session I hold on the first Sunday of each month.'
Disha nodded slowly and left the pedas anyway.

What are Nandini's Sunday hours?
10 to 12, only those.
What might Disha have been feeling when she arrived?
Disha was hopeful and a little anxious, wanting help for her daughter in Class 11.
Why is it wise for Nandini to take only two students?
Last year five students meant cancelled Sundays and rushed help; two lets her give each student reliable time.
How might Disha's daughter be affected by the answer?
She has to wait until January, but gets a reliable place then and the monthly doubt session meanwhile.

Saturday. Six months since I started meeting Sangeeta, so today's session was a review. We went through the list from January. Done: portfolio site, two mock interviews, and a first proper offer letter. Not done: the open-source contribution. Sangeeta said she still wants it, so it stays, but on her own with a check-in from me. Then I raised the thing I'd been putting off: maybe we don't need regular sessions anymore. I worried it would sound like I was pulling away. Sangeeta grinned and said she'd been thinking the same and would rather message me when stuck. So we're moving to one catch-up every two months, plus messages anytime. Strange, but it feels like a finish line, not a door closing. — Naveen

The open-source contribution was not finished.
What did Naveen worry about when raising the change?
Naveen worried that it would sound like Naveen was pulling away.

Naveen could offer a one-off session before any big decision, such as a job choice, since it keeps support available without a fixed rota.

Sangeeta probably sees it as a good step, since she had been thinking the same and would rather message when stuck.

Six months after they first met at the tea stall outside the Anand bus depot, Chinmay and Charu sat in the same spot with the same notebook. Charu had started a small milk delivery service for thirty homes; Chinmay, who had run one before, had been meeting her every other Saturday.
'Let's look at what you wanted in January,' Chinmay said, opening the first page. 'A route that runs without you on the scooter every day. Done, you have two delivery boys. Books that balance each month. Done. Fifty homes by June.' 'Forty-two,' Charu said. 'Close enough to handle myself.'
Chinmay closed the notebook. 'Then I think we stop the Saturdays. Not because I'm leaving. Because you don't need them.' Charu looked unsure, then smiled. 'Call you if the cows go on strike?' 'Any time.'

How many homes does Charu deliver to now?
Forty-two.
What might Charu have been feeling when she looked unsure?
Charu may have felt a moment of worry at losing the regular support, then pride in no longer needing it.
What else could Chinmay do to keep the door open?
Chinmay could suggest a check-in in a few months, and make clear that Charu can call when something big comes up.
How might Chinmay feel closing the notebook?
Chinmay likely feels satisfied, seeing the end of the Saturdays as proof the mentoring worked.

At a Saturday workshop in a community centre in Indore, Tanvir, a software tester, was handed a sheet titled 'What keeps pulling you?' Vinita, the facilitator, asked everyone to list problems they kept reading about or raising without being asked. Tanvir wrote quickly: village school dropouts, water quality in the old city, and, after a pause, lonely elderly neighbours. Vinita's second question was, 'Which of these fit what you can actually do?' Tanvir crossed out the third, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have, and circled the first. 'I can build simple tools, and I keep thinking about the school in my grandfather's village.' Vinita asked one more thing: 'Whose voices haven't you heard yet?' Tanvir wrote it as the first line under the circle: talk to the teachers.

What was the title of the sheet Tanvir was handed?
The sheet was titled 'What keeps pulling you?'
How did Tanvir feel about the third problem, and why was it crossed out?
Tanvir cared about it, but felt unequipped, since it needed skills Tanvir didn't have.
What other approach could Tanvir use to test the first choice?
Tanvir could volunteer for a month with a local group working on school dropouts, since real contact shows whether the interest lasts.
How might Vinita see Tanvir's choice?
Vinita probably sees a sensible one, joining a real concern to real skills, with a first step of listening to teachers.

Read this:

Dear Omkar,
You asked what I meant by 'finding my project'. I've been doing an exercise for three weeks, and I think I'm close.
First I wrote down every problem that kept pulling at me, the things I read about at midnight: girls dropping out of school in our district, water tankers in summer, old people alone in flats. Then, next to each, I wrote what I'm actually good at. I'm a data analyst. I'm patient with spreadsheets. I can't dig wells. I don't know teaching.
Where they overlap: school dropout data. The district office publishes it, but nobody reads it. I could help a local NGO spot which villages lose girls after Class 8, and why.
Before I choose, I'm going to call two NGOs next week and ask if that's even useful.
Keerthana

What problems did Keerthana list?
Girls dropping out of school in the district, water tankers in summer, and old people alone in flats.
How does Keerthana seem to feel about being 'close'?
Keerthana feels hopeful and clearer, having found an overlap between a problem that matters and a real skill.
Why is calling two NGOs before choosing wise?
It checks whether the idea is actually useful to the people doing the work, before Keerthana commits time to it.
How might a local NGO see Keerthana's offer?
An NGO might welcome free help making sense of data it has no time to read, if it fits the work.

Read this:

Seema, you asked why I'm not joining the tree-planting drive everyone's doing. It's not that I don't care. I'm Urmila, and I spent last month asking myself two questions. One: which problems do I keep coming back to, even when nobody asks me? For me it's clean water in the villages near Nashik, where my grandmother lives, and children who can't read in Class 5. Two: what can I actually do that others can't? I'm a civil engineer. I understand pipes, pumps and tanks. Teaching reading? I'd be a beginner. So water is where my skills meet what I care about. Next month I'm visiting my grandmother's village with a notebook to see what the water committee needs. Trees are good. They're just not my project.

Which two problems does Urmila keep coming back to?
Clean water in the villages near Nashik and children who can't read in Class 5.
How does Urmila feel about not joining the tree-planting drive?
Urmila feels calm and sure, caring about the cause but settled that water is where Urmila can help most.
Why is visiting the village with a notebook a good next step?
It lets Urmila learn what the water committee really needs before designing anything.
How might the village water committee see Urmila's visit?
They may welcome an engineer who comes to listen first, especially one with family ties to the village.

Saturday, 9 pm. First class done. Twenty students from classes eight to ten in the school near my aunt's village crammed into one room with six borrowed laptops. Neelam, the science teacher who let me use the room, sat at the back. I'd planned an hour on variables; it took forty minutes because half the group couldn't type yet, so we switched to drawing flowcharts on paper and typing in pairs. Learned already: pairs work, short tasks work, my slides don't. The power went out twice, and the kids clapped in the dark when it came back. I'm not planning anything big yet. Four more Saturdays, then I'll write down what worked and only then decide what next. Tired feet, full head. — Farida

How many laptops were there?
There were six borrowed laptops.
How does Farida feel at the end of the day?
Farida feels tired but energised, with tired feet and a full head from what was learned.
What other approach could Farida use before the next class?
Farida could ask Neelam and a few students what they want to learn, since it shows what is worth teaching before more slides are made.
How might Neelam see the class?
Neelam probably sees a useful start, since twenty students turned up and stayed engaged even when the power went out.

messages.content:
Read this:

Every Sunday morning, Ramesh took the 7 a.m. bus from Kolhapur to his native village and walked to the zilla parishad school. Omkar Sir, the maths teacher, unlocked the one room with computers: four old desktops and a borrowed laptop. Twenty children from Classes 6 to 8 were already waiting on the steps.
Ramesh didn't have a big plan. He had a notebook where he wrote, after each class, what worked and what didn't. Week 2: children share better in pairs than in fours. Week 4: games work, lectures don't. Week 6: power cut, so paper puzzles. Week 9: two girls built a simple quiz without help.
Omkar Sir started staying for the whole class. 'If this keeps going,' he said in week ten, 'I could run a Wednesday session myself.' Ramesh wrote that down too.

What happened in week 9?
Two girls built a simple quiz without help.
What does Omkar Sir staying for the whole class suggest?
It suggests Omkar Sir became interested and hopeful, enough to consider running a session himself.
Why is Ramesh's notebook a good part of the pilot?
It records what works, like pairs and games, so any bigger plan is built on real lessons.
How might the children experience the Sunday classes?
They get hands-on games and puzzles, and some, like the two girls, gain confidence building things themselves.

messages.content:
Read this:

For eight months Kiran told anyone who'd listen about the plan to transform education across the state. There was a forty-slide deck, three logo options, and a name argued over with Manoj, a friend, on long tea breaks. Kiran also had a full-time job and only Sunday mornings free. Whenever Manoj asked, 'What can we do this month?' Kiran said the idea was too big for small steps. Teaching one class felt silly next to a whole state. One Sunday a heavy monsoon kept the two indoors, and Manoj asked to see the calendar: not one meeting with a school, not one test of an idea. The deck was polished, and nothing else existed. Kiran closed the laptop and said nothing for a while.

How many logo options did Kiran have?
Kiran had three logo options.
Why did Kiran resist small steps?
Kiran felt the dream was so large that teaching one class seemed silly next to a whole state, so any first step felt too small.
What other approach could Kiran use to get started?
Kiran could pick one school and run a small pilot on a Sunday morning, since a real class would teach more than another version of the deck.
How might Manoj see the deck and the months of talk?
Manoj probably sees a lot of effort with nothing tested and feels frustrated, and asking to see the calendar shows worry for Kiran.

messages.content:
Read this:

In his rented room in Andheri, Eshaan had forty slides titled 'Transforming Education Across Maharashtra'. Three logo versions. A mission statement he rewrote every week. A plan for 10,000 schools in five years.
It was October. He had started in March.
His friend Rehana, a schoolteacher, came over and scrolled through the deck. 'It's beautiful,' she said. 'How many students have you taught?'
'None yet. I need funding first. And a team. And the app.'
'My school has a free slot on Saturdays. Twelve kids who need help with maths. You could start next week.'
Eshaan looked at the forty slides. Twelve kids felt almost embarrassing next to 10,000 schools. 'That's too small to matter,' he said.
Rehana closed the laptop. 'Eshaan, you've spent seven months on slides. Twelve is more than zero.'

How many schools did Eshaan's plan cover?
10,000 schools in five years.
Why did twelve kids feel 'almost embarrassing' to Eshaan?
Next to his grand plan, a small start made Eshaan feel small and a little ashamed, as if it didn't count.
What would you advise Eshaan to do next Saturday?
Accept Rehana's offer and teach the twelve kids, learning what works before building anything bigger.
How might Rehana see the forty slides?
Rehana admires them but is frustrated that seven months of planning have helped no student yet.

'Kavitha, how long have you been working on this "Water for Every Village" thing?'
'Eight months, Chandrika. The website's almost done. And the brand book.'
'Brand book?'
'Colours, fonts. We need to look serious when we go to big donors.'
'How many villages have water because of it?'
'...It's not launched yet. It's a national plan, it can't start small.'
'Why not?'
'Because one village doesn't change anything.'
'It changes things for that village. Paati's village has had a broken handpump since March. The panchayat just needs someone to follow up, and one mechanic.'
Kavitha looked at her laptop, at the logo glowing on the screen. 'That's not what the vision is.'
'Then the vision will stay on the screen,' Chandrika said gently.

Since when has the handpump in Paati's village been broken?
Since March.
How might Kavitha feel looking at the logo on the screen?
Kavitha seems torn and defensive, attached to the big vision and uneasy that nothing has actually started.
What small first step could Kavitha take?
Kavitha could help Paati's village get the handpump fixed by following up with the panchayat and finding one mechanic.
How does the plan look to Chandrika?
Chandrika sees eight months of branding with no real help given, and gently worries the vision will never leave the screen.

Mridul: Back from the village. So glad I went before ordering books.
Bidisha: Tell me. What did they say?

Mridul: Everyone said the same thing: kids can't study after dark. Power cuts, and one bulb at home.
Bidisha: Not more books? 😮
Mridul: Books came third. First lighting, second a quiet room with a table.
Bidisha: So the library becomes a study room with a lamp?

Bidisha: Then what are you buying first?
Mridul: Two solar lamps and six mats. Books later, when the kids tell me what they want.

How many parents and teachers did Mridul talk to?
Mridul talked to eight parents and three teachers.
How did Mridul feel about going to the village first?
Mridul felt glad and relieved to have listened before ordering books, since it changed the whole plan.
What could Mridul do next to check the plan works?
Mridul could open the room for a week and ask families what changes they notice, since real use shows what to adjust.

Anjali had collected three hundred donated books in her Pune flat for a library in her mother's village near Wardha. Before she hired a tempo, she went to the village for a week with a notebook, not the books.
She sat on verandahs with parents and spent afternoons with Madhuri Tai, the headmistress. She asked one thing again and again: 'What stops the children from studying in the evening?'
Nobody said books. 'Light,' said a mother whose house got power for four hours a day. 'A place,' said Madhuri Tai. 'Five children in one room with the TV on. Where will they sit?'
Anjali went back to Pune and changed the plan. The first step would be a solar-lit room at the school, open from six to nine every evening. The books would come later, a hundred at a time.

How many donated books had Anjali collected?
Three hundred donated books.
How might Anjali have felt when nobody said books?
Anjali was probably surprised and a little deflated at first, then grateful to learn before spending on the wrong thing.
Why was going with a notebook instead of the books a wise first step?
It let the community say what they needed, so the plan fits real problems like light and space.
How might the mother whose house has power four hours a day see the new plan?
She'd likely feel heard and relieved, since a lit room gives her children somewhere to study in the evening.

Sofia had grown up in Cape Town and wanted to give something back to the small town in the Eastern Cape where her grandmother had taught. Her first idea was a library with new books. But before ordering anything, she spent two weeks there, sitting in on classes and visiting families after school.
Lindiwe, a teacher at the primary school, walked her through the township at dusk. 'Look,' she said. Windows were dark; many homes had no electricity once the prepaid meter ran out. 'The children have books from school. What they don't have is light and a quiet table.'
Sofia rewrote her plan on the drive back. First, a room at the community hall with solar lamps and tables, open every weekday evening, with a volunteer to keep it safe. Books would follow, chosen with the teachers.

Where had Sofia's grandmother taught?
In a small town in the Eastern Cape.
How might Sofia have felt walking with Lindiwe at dusk?
Sofia may have felt humbled and a little uneasy, seeing that her first idea didn't match what the children most needed.
What else could Sofia do before opening the room?
She could check with parents about the best evening hours and safe routes home, so the room fits family life.
How might Lindiwe see Sofia's changed plan?
Lindiwe would likely feel respected and hopeful, seeing that her observation shaped the plan.

Sunday. Been thinking about what happens to the evening reading circle if I take the Pune job next year, or just get swamped at work. Right now it's me: I hold the key, the booklist and the phone numbers. That isn't a project, it's a habit of mine. So this month I asked Minakshi, who lives two lanes from the hall and comes every day, to start opening up and leading the story hour. Showed how the register works, where the books go, who to call about the hall. Also asked five parents for a small monthly amount, enough for the hall's electricity bill. Four said yes. On Thursday Minakshi read to the kids alone while I stood outside. It wobbled, and it worked. — Manoj

The seed library in Kharkhoda's panchayat hall was only a steel cupboard and a register, but forty families now swapped seeds there each sowing season. Simran had built it over two years. Now the nursing post in the district hospital was hers, and she would be there six days a week.
Sitting on the hall steps, she counted on her fingers. Who opens the cupboard in June when I'm on a night shift? Who writes in the register? Who buys the paper packets when they run out?
Arnab, the dairy man's son, had helped her sort millet seeds every Saturday. That week she stood beside him while he filled the register himself. Then she went to the milk cooperative meeting and asked if a small share of each month's fund could buy packets and ink. The members agreed.
"Now it belongs to the village," Arnab said.

Where was the seed library kept?
It was a steel cupboard and a register in Kharkhoda's panchayat hall.
What was Simran feeling as she counted on her fingers on the hall steps?
She was worried that the library would fall apart once she was on night shifts, and she was checking each job that only she did.
Which other step could make the library even safer if Arnab also becomes busy?
Training a second helper alongside Arnab would help, so the cupboard and register never depend on one person again.
How might the milk cooperative members see Simran's request?
They may feel the library is now partly theirs, because a small share of their monthly fund keeps it stocked, which gives them a reason to protect it.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Lalit. Three years ago, after a good bonus, I paid for a computer lab in a school in a district I'd read about. Twenty machines, new desks, a ribbon-cutting. I was proud. I had never asked the school what it needed. Power there went off for most of the day with no backup, and no one on the staff had been taught to use the machines. When I visited a year later, Pradeep, the headmaster, walked me into the room. The screens were under plastic sheets and the door was kept locked to protect them. He said the teachers would have preferred a roof that didn't leak. That stayed with me. I had made a gift that fitted my picture of help, not their school.

How many machines were in the lab?
There were twenty machines in the lab.
What was Lalit feeling at the ribbon-cutting, and how did it change at the later visit?
Lalit felt proud at the ribbon-cutting, but at the later visit felt regretful and humbled on seeing the covered screens and locked door.
What could Lalit have done differently before paying for the lab?
Lalit could have asked the school what it needed and started small with backup power and teacher training, since a fit with the local situation decides whether equipment gets used.
How might Pradeep have felt about the lab?
Pradeep was probably grateful but frustrated, keeping the room locked to protect it and mentioning that teachers wanted a roof that didn't leak.

Read this:

School log, Thursday.
Mr Shankar came today to see the lab he gave us last June. Twelve computers, new tables, a banner with his company's name. The room has been locked since Diwali. Power comes for about four hours a day here, mostly after school, and there is no inverter. None of our teachers has used these machines before, so nobody felt confident to take a class in there.
I unlocked it for him. Dust covers on every screen. A few Class 6 children pressed their faces to the window glass as we stood inside.
He was quiet for a long time, then asked why nobody had told him. I said we did not want to seem ungrateful.
Next step: I have asked him to meet our four teachers on Saturday and hear what they actually need before anything else is bought.
— Parveen, Head Teacher

How long has the lab been locked?
The room has been locked since Diwali.
What might Shankar have been feeling when he stood quietly in the dusty lab?
He was likely shocked and disappointed, seeing that his gift had been unused for months while children could only look in through the window.
What approach could Shankar have tried before buying the computers?
He could have asked the teachers first about power and training, and planned a backup supply and teacher sessions along with the machines.
How do the Class 6 children at the window experience the unused lab?
For them the lab is something to look at but never use, which may feel like a promise that was not kept.

Tuesday night
Went back to Bhimpur school today, first time since we opened the lab in March. I was carrying the photo from the opening ceremony on my phone. All ten tablets charging, children smiling.
Avni Ma'am, the maths teacher, walked me to the room. Locked. Inside, the tablets were stacked in their box. "Power goes by eleven most days," she said. "And nobody showed us how to use the lesson app. The children kept asking. After a while they stopped."
I kept saying, "But we raised the money in three weeks!" as if that fixed anything.
On the bus back I did the maths. The fundraising, the travel, the ceremony, and maybe six hours of use in total.
I planned this from my flat in the city. I never once asked Avni Ma'am what the school needed. Tomorrow I'm going to call her and ask.
— Varun

What does Avni Ma'am say happens to the power most days?
She says the power goes by eleven most days.
How can you tell Varun felt ashamed on the bus back?
Varun works out that all the effort bought maybe six hours of use and admits never once asking Avni Ma'am what the school needed.
What else could Varun have done first, and why would it help?
Varun could have visited and asked the teachers about power and training before raising money, so the plan fit what the school could actually use.
How might Avni Ma'am feel about the unused tablets?
She may feel frustrated and a little embarrassed, since the children kept asking and the teachers were never shown how to use the lesson app.

In a village hall outside Jhansi, Sachin ran a Saturday tuition centre for forty children. Every month he sat down with Preeti, a volunteer teacher, and a notebook. They counted attendance from the register, marked the short maths test, and asked each child for one line on what they liked and disliked. In March the reading circle had eleven children on average and scores had barely moved. The children's notes said, 'Story time is the best.' Maths practice had steady attendance and rising scores. The two decided: drop the drawing class, which had few children and no change in anything; change reading to use stories; keep maths as it was. Sachin pinned the numbers on the hall wall. 'We'll look again in April,' he said.

How many children did the reading circle have on average in March?
The reading circle had eleven children on average.
What does Sachin want from looking at the numbers again in April?
Sachin wants decisions to rest on evidence and to keep adjusting, which shows a steady commitment to the centre.
What other kind of evidence could Sachin add to the monthly numbers?
Sachin could ask parents at pick-up time what they notice at home, since families may see changes that scores and registers miss.
How might Preeti see the decision to drop the drawing class?
Preeti probably sees it as fair because the numbers back it, though may feel sorry for the few children who enjoyed it.

On the first Monday of every month, Priscila spread three sheets across the kitchen table of the community flat in Porto. Attendance from the sign-in book. The short maths quiz the children took each Friday. And the feedback cards, where they drew a face and wrote one sentence.
Ulla, the volunteer who ran the chess hour, peered over her shoulder. "So? Are we keeping chess?"
Priscila tapped the numbers. "Chess has had three children for two months. The cards say it's 'fine.' Homework help has fourteen, and quiz scores went up from the last month."
"That's harsh on chess."
"Not stopping it yet. Let's try it on Saturday morning for one month instead. If it's still three, we stop and put you on homework help."
Ulla sighed, then smiled. "Fair. You've got the numbers."

What three records did Priscila spread across the table?
Attendance from the sign-in book, the Friday maths quiz scores and the children's feedback cards.
What might Ulla have been feeling when she asked if they were keeping chess?
She was probably nervous and a little protective, because the chess hour was hers and the numbers could mean it would end.
Why is a one-month trial a better choice than stopping chess at once?
It gives the activity a fair chance to recover under a new time, and the same monthly numbers will show clearly whether to keep or stop it.
How might the children who come to homework help be affected by these monthly checks?
They benefit, because effort goes where attendance and quiz scores show it is working, and more volunteers may join their group.

The noticeboard in the Tolichowki community centre had a new chart every month. Vinita, who ran the Saturday coding class, filled it in herself. Rows for each activity: coding, spoken English, the art corner. Columns for how many came, the end-of-month test average, and the tally of thumbs-up and thumbs-down slips.
In the September review, Zainab, a second-year volunteer, read the English row aloud. "Attendance fell from twenty-two to nine. Slips say it clashes with Friday prayers."
"Then the problem is the timing, not the class," Vinita said. "Test scores for the nine who came are good."
She moved English to Sunday afternoon. The art corner, which had full attendance but no tests, stayed as it was.
In October the chart showed English back at twenty. Zainab drew a small star beside it on the board.

How far did attendance in the English class fall?
Attendance fell from twenty-two to nine.
How can you tell Zainab felt pleased in October?
She drew a small star beside the English row after the chart showed attendance back at twenty, showing she was proud and relieved. 😊
What would you change first if the English attendance had not come back after the move?
I would talk to a few of the students who stopped coming, because the slips give a clue but a short conversation could show a reason the numbers miss.
How do the students who pray on Fridays experience Vinita's change?
They no longer have to choose between prayers and class, so they may feel included and more willing to keep coming.

'Before the donation drive, I want us registered properly,' said Lakshmi, putting a folder on Shreya's desk.
'Good,' said Shreya, a lawyer at the legal aid clinic. 'I'll draft the trust papers with you. And the bank account goes in the trust's name, not yours.'
'And every rupee goes in a ledger the same day?'
'Yes, with a receipt number. A chartered accountant should look at the books once a year.'
'Can donors see the accounts?'
'They should. A short summary on your page each quarter.'
Lakshmi hesitated. 'Won't some people think we're showing off?'
'People give more when they can see where it goes. And clear records help whenever the authorities ask.'
Lakshmi nodded and wrote on the folder: Ledger. Receipts. Quarterly summary.

Whose name should the bank account be in?
The bank account goes in the trust's name, not Lakshmi's.
What worried Lakshmi about sharing the accounts?
Lakshmi was worried that some people would think the trust was showing off.
What other step could Lakshmi add to keep donors informed?
Lakshmi could invite one donor each quarter to look over the ledger in person, since seeing the books first-hand builds trust.
How might a donor see the quarterly summary?
A donor would likely feel trusted and reassured, and more willing to give again, because they can see where the money goes. 🙂

I'm Ramesh, and for the first year the Ward 9 Library ran out of a biscuit tin. People handed me cash at the gate, and I wrote amounts in a school notebook when I remembered.
Then a retired teacher sent a large cheque and asked for a receipt with a registration number. I didn't have one. I felt like a fraud, though I'd never taken a rupee.
My friend Anjali works in a law office, and she introduced me to a lawyer who helped us register a small trust. It took two months of forms. After that, every rupee went into the trust's bank account, every expense had a bill, and the treasurer and I both signed.
Each quarter we sent donors a one-page statement: money in, books bought, rent paid. The retired teacher wrote back, "Now I can tell my friends to give too."

Where did the library keep money during its first year?
It ran out of a biscuit tin, with amounts written in a school notebook.
How did Ramesh feel when asked for a receipt with a registration number?
Ramesh felt like a fraud and ashamed, even though no money had ever been taken, because there was nothing official to show.
Which other safeguard could the library add as it grows, and why?
It could ask an outside accountant to check the books once a year, so donors see an independent view and not only the library's own statement.
How does the retired teacher see the library after the quarterly statements start?
The teacher trusts it enough to encourage friends to donate, because the money in and out is now visible.

I suggested she also put the registration number on every receipt. She wrote it down at once.

Gurpreet, the volunteer treasurer, keeps a ledger with every bill pasted in beside the entry.

Gurpreet may feel steadier and more responsible, with a clear ledger and bills that protect the treasurer if anyone asks questions.

Read this:

I'm Rekha, and last winter I wanted to start a tiffin delivery service for students in our area.

I read them in a row and felt sick. Every line seemed equally likely, equally fatal. I never sorted them, never asked which ones mattered.
My friend Nilesh asked a week later, "So when do you start?" I said I was still researching risks.

Read this:

In the small tuition room above the kirana shop in Ramgarh, Trisha's maths test came back with 38 marks. Again.
Her cousin Tarun, home from college, sat beside her. "What went wrong?"
"Silly mistakes."
"Why silly mistakes?"
She thought. "I was hurrying."
"Why hurrying?"
"The last questions were left, and ten minutes."
"Why were they left?"
Trisha flipped back to page one. The first five questions, simple equations, had taken her almost half the time. "Because I'm slow on the beginning part. I check each one three times."
Tarun nodded. "So the problem isn't silly mistakes."
"It's speed on easy questions." She grabbed her rough book. "If I practise those till they're fast, I'll have time at the end."
That week, she did twenty quick equations every evening before dinner.

How many marks did Trisha get on the test?
Trisha's maths test came back with 38 marks.
How might Trisha have felt when she flipped back to page one?
She probably felt surprised and a little relieved, finding the real cause was slowness on easy questions, not carelessness.
What else could Trisha do in the next test, and why?
She could check easy questions once, not three times, and go back to them at the end if time is left.
How does Tarun see Trisha's discovery?
Tarun is pleased to see her find the deeper cause herself, which is why he just nods and lets her work out the fix.

Nilesh had been late to the eight o'clock lecture nine times in a month, and Binita, the hostel warden, asked him to stop by her office. Instead of scolding, she asked, 'Why are you late?' 'I wake up late.' 'Why?' 'I sleep late.' 'Why?' He shrugged. 'I scroll on my phone in bed until two.' 'And why do you scroll?' 'I just keep doing it. It's a habit.' Nilesh looked at the floor. He didn't need a louder alarm; he needed the phone out of reach. That night he put the charger on a shelf in the corridor, beyond the reach of his bed. By Friday he was in his seat at ten to eight.

How many times was Nilesh late in a month?
Nilesh was late nine times in a month.

Nilesh probably felt embarrassed and a little uncomfortable admitting that scrolling was a habit he couldn't stop.
What other step could help Nilesh keep to the change?
Nilesh could ask a roommate to check that the phone is charging in the corridor at night, since a small promise to someone else helps a new habit last.

Dear Jatin bhai,
You asked how I stopped getting marked late at the hostel gate every morning. The warden had warned me twice, and I was sure I just needed a louder alarm.
Then I tried asking why, properly. Why am I late? Because I can't get up at the alarm. Why? Because I'm exhausted. Why? Because I sleep at two. Why? Because I'm on my phone in bed till then. Why? Because I scroll every night without deciding to. It's a habit.
So a louder alarm was never the answer. The phone in bed was.
Now I charge my phone on the study table across the room, and I don't bring it to bed. The first three nights were hard. By the second week I was asleep by midnight.
I've been on time for eleven days straight.
Irfan

Where does Irfan now charge the phone?
On the study table across the room.
How did Irfan feel during the first three nights?
Irfan found them hard, probably restless and tempted to reach for the phone, before the new habit settled.
Why was moving the phone better than getting a louder alarm?
It fixed the root cause, late-night scrolling, instead of the symptom, so Irfan actually slept enough to wake on time.
How might the warden see Irfan's eleven days on time?
The warden may be relieved and pleased that the warnings led to a real change, not just excuses.

Sharmila, you want to know how your cousin Abhinav became the first one at breakfast? It's a bit embarrassing, but okay.
Second semester, I was late for the 8 a.m. lecture almost every day. My attendance was falling. I kept blaming the hostel alarm, the noisy corridor, everything.
Then one night I sat down and asked myself why five times. Late, because I oversleep. Oversleep, because I'm tired. Tired, because I sleep at 2.30. Sleep late, because I'm on my phone. On my phone, because I scroll without noticing, every night, out of habit.
The alarm was never the problem. The phone was.
So I did one simple thing. The charger went into the corridor socket outside our room, and the phone stayed there all night. My roommate thought I was mad.
Three weeks now. Asleep by twelve. Not a single late mark.

Into the corridor socket outside the room.

Abhinav felt a bit embarrassed, admitting that blaming the alarm and the corridor had hidden the real reason.

I'm Ramesh, and I'll tell you about the outage I'm least proud of. A config change took our site down for an hour. In the meeting I asked once, 'Why did it go down?' and the answer was, 'Kamal pushed a wrong value.' Everyone nodded, relieved to have an answer. I told Kamal to be more careful, and we moved on. Kamal was quiet for a week. Then, six weeks later, someone else pushed a wrong value and the site went down again. That's when it hit me: I had never asked why a wrong value could reach the live site at all. No test caught it, and nobody was clearly in charge of reviewing config. Kamal wasn't the cause. Kamal was just the person nearest the button.

How long after the first outage did the second one happen?
The second outage happened six weeks later.
How might Kamal have felt after being told to be more careful?
Kamal probably felt ashamed and unfairly singled out, shown by being quiet for a week.
What other approach could Ramesh have used in the first meeting?
Ramesh could have kept asking why until a process cause appeared, such as why no test caught the wrong value and who reviews config.
How might Kamal's teammates have felt at the first meeting?
They were probably relieved at first to have a simple answer, though the second outage would leave them uneasy.

I'm Kashish, I sit two desks from Usha's team, and I watched their outage meeting through the glass on Tuesday.
The payments page had been down for three hours on Monday. Usha, the team lead, stood at the whiteboard and wrote one question: Why did it go down?
Someone said Arvind had pushed a wrong setting. Everyone turned to Arvind. He stared at the table. Usha wrote "human error, Arvind" and underlined it. The meeting ended in twelve minutes.
Nobody asked why a wrong setting could go live without a test, or why the review didn't catch it.
Three weeks later, the page went down again. A different person, a different setting, the same kind of mistake.
I saw Arvind at the coffee machine that day. He said quietly, "At least it wasn't me this time." He didn't look relieved.

How long had the payments page been down on Monday?
The payments page had been down for three hours.
What does Arvind staring at the table suggest?
It suggests he felt ashamed and singled out, as the whole room turned to him.
Which approach would suit Usha's team better?
Asking why several times, beyond the person, to find why an untested setting could go live and why review missed it, then fixing that.
How does Kashish see the outage meeting?
Kashish sees a quick meeting that blamed one person and skipped the deeper causes, and notices it led to the same outage again.

Monday. The booking app for the clinic chain went down during the morning rush, and patients could not book for two hours. By noon Hemant, the engineering manager, had the answer. "Jyoti deployed the change without checking the config. Human error."
Jyoti said nothing in the meeting. That evening she sat alone at her desk long after everyone left.
Wednesday. Hemant sent a short report up to the director: cause identified, engineer counselled, closed. Nobody asked why there was no automatic test for the config, or why the reviewer approved it in two minutes.
Eighteen days later. The app went down again on a Saturday. This time it was a senior engineer's change, the same kind of config mistake.
Jyoti read the alert on her phone at home and felt something between relief and anger. It had never been only her.

How long were patients unable to book on Monday?
Patients could not book for two hours.
What was Jyoti feeling when she read the alert eighteen days later?
She felt something between relief and anger, realising the problem had never been only her.
What would you change first in how Hemant handled the outage?
Ask why several times until reaching the missing config test and the rushed review, and fix those instead of blaming one engineer.
How might the patients be affected by the team stopping at blame?
Patients face the same outage again, because the real cause was never fixed.

messages.content:
Read this:

Chetan, you were on leave during the outage review, so let Payal tell you what happened, because I think we finally did it right.
Last time, we blamed Suresh and moved on, and it happened again. This time I said, nobody's name goes on the board till we've asked why five times.
Why did the site go down? A bad config went live. Why did it go live? It passed review. Why did review pass it? The reviewer only saw the code diff, not the config. Why? Because config changes aren't shown in review at all. Why? Because our deployment script never included them.
So the cause wasn't a person. It was a gap in our process.
We added an automatic check that stops any deployment if the config fails a test. Suresh wrote it himself, actually. Two months now. No repeat.

Who wrote the automatic check?
Suresh wrote it himself.
How might Payal feel about this outage review compared with the last one?
Payal seems relieved and quietly proud, believing the team finally did it right by finding a process gap instead of blaming someone.

They could review other steps in the deployment script for similar gaps, since one missing check suggests there may be others.
How might Suresh see the new review?
Suresh, who was blamed last time, may feel respected and relieved, and writing the fix himself suggests he felt trusted.

I'm Farhan, and I'm new in the QA team, so I mostly sat and watched Ishita's outage review on Thursday.
I'd heard the last one had ended in five minutes with somebody blamed. This time Ishita put a rule on the board first: "No names. Just why."
Then she kept asking. Why did the orders stop? The database connection broke. Why? A setting was changed. Why wasn't it caught? The test suite doesn't cover settings. Why? Nobody owned that part. Why? It was never on anyone's checklist.
It took forty minutes. People kept wanting to say who did it, and she kept pulling them back to why.
At the end, she assigned an automatic settings test to be added to every deployment, and put a name next to the task, not next to the mistake.
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked tired but satisfied.

Monday. Tenzin came home from school, dropped his shoes in the doorway, and his older sister Binita tripped over them carrying the laundry. "Every single day!" she said.
That night Tenzin lay in bed thinking. He always forgot because he was thinking about snacks, not shoes. So he needed something to remind him that wasn't his memory.
Tuesday. He made a rule and said it out loud at the door: "If I see my shoes on the floor, then they go on the rack." He put them there. It felt silly.
Wednesday. He came in, saw the shoes, and his hands moved before he thought about it. Rack.
Two weeks later, Binita came home and stopped. There were no shoes in the doorway at all. "Did Amma make you do this?"
"No," Tenzin said, eating his biscuit. "The shoes remind me."

The night before, Kashish lay on the terrace floor going over it in his head. Someone will say "let's skip", it always happens on Fridays. If they do, then I say, "I have a test next period," and I walk to class. No long explaining, no arguing. At recess the next day Preeti bumped his shoulder. "Skip physics? The ground's free."

Kashish's mouth was dry, but the words were already waiting. "I've got a test next period. Catch you after." He picked up his bag and left. It was a small quiz, but a real one, and his hands only started shaking when he reached the corridor.

Kashish said the sentence aloud twice to the water tank on the terrace.

messages.content:

Dear Lokesh,
You asked how I handle the gang at the back gate who bunk the last period. Here's my secret, and it's not bravery.
Last month they asked me to come to the arcade with them during Hindi. I stood there with my mouth open, didn't know what to say, and nearly went, just because saying no felt awkward.
That night I thought about it. The problem wasn't that I wanted to go. It was that I had no words ready. So I decided: if they ask me to skip class, then I say, "I've got a test, catch you after," and walk to class. Same words every time. No explaining.
Yesterday they asked again. I said it without even thinking and walked off. Nobody even argued.
Try it. Pick your line before they ask.
Baljeet

What line did Baljeet decide to use?
"I've got a test, catch you after."
How did Baljeet feel the first time the gang asked?
Baljeet felt awkward and flustered, standing with an open mouth and nearly going along just to avoid saying no.
Why does deciding the words beforehand help?
Because in the moment there's no need to think or explain, so saying no feels easy instead of awkward.
How might Lokesh feel reading this letter?
Lokesh may feel encouraged and less alone, with a simple plan to try against the same pressure.

messages.content:

Kalyani, you asked on your channel how teenagers deal with peer pressure, so here's Zubin's actual method. It's boring, but it works.
In Class 11 my friends started skipping the Saturday practical and going to the lake. They'd ask right outside the lab, with everyone watching. The first two times I made up long excuses and they laughed. The third time I just went. And I hated it the whole afternoon.
So I sat down and planned it like a sum. When does it happen? Saturday, outside the lab. What do they say? "Come on, bunk." What will I say? "Can't, test prep, see you later." Then I walk in. No reasons, no debate.
The next Saturday they asked. I said my line and walked into the lab before anyone could reply. My heart was thumping, but it was easy.
Having the words ready is the whole trick.

Right outside the lab, with everyone watching.

Zubin hated it the whole afternoon, feeling unhappy about giving in.

Bhupen's hostel room in the Tezpur college was always noisy in the evenings, and his flashcards for the English entrance test sat in a rubber band on the shelf, untouched. Every night he promised himself he'd do them. Every night he didn't.
His senior Naveen said, "You brush your teeth every morning without fail, right?"
"Obviously."
"Then tie the cards to that. After brushing, five cards. Nothing else."
The next morning Bhupen brushed his teeth at the corridor sink, came back, and picked up five cards from the stack by his toothbrush mug. Five words. Two minutes.
By the end of the month, the rubber band had moved to a second stack: words he knew. He hadn't missed a single morning, because he hadn't missed a single brushing.

How many cards did Bhupen do after brushing?
Five cards.
How had Bhupen been feeling about the untouched flashcards?
He was probably guilty and frustrated, promising himself every night and never doing them.
Why did linking the cards to brushing work better than promising to do them at night?
Because brushing already happens every morning without fail, so it reminds him automatically, while the noisy evenings kept pushing the cards aside.
How does Naveen's suggestion look to Bhupen at first?
It seems almost too simple at first, but it gives Bhupen a small habit he actually keeps.

In the small flat in Taipei, Wei shared a bathroom with his sister Xin and was always rushing in the mornings. His language-exam flashcards lived in a drawer. He meant to study at night, but by night he was too tired.

So he put the flashcard box beside the sink. Every morning, toothbrush back in the cup, then five cards, reading each one aloud while the kettle boiled.
After three weeks, he'd gone through the whole box once. He told Xin, "I never had to remember. The toothbrush remembers for me."

He put the flashcard box beside the sink.

On Sunday night, Amandeep, the new ward manager at the city hospital's admin block, typed out her weekly plan. It was four pages of if-then rules. If a nurse calls in sick, then check the float list. If the supply order is late, then call the vendor before ten. If a doctor asks for a meeting, then offer Tuesday or Thursday. If... Thirty-eight rules in all.
On Wednesday, everything happened at once. Two staff called in sick, the pharmacy delivery didn't come, and a senior doctor wanted a meeting right now.
Baljeet, her assistant, found her at the desk flipping through the four pages. "Which rule is this?"
"I don't know," she said. "I can't find anything."
By noon she had stopped looking at the pages altogether. She was just answering whoever was loudest, the same as last month.

How many rules did Amandeep write?
Thirty-eight rules in all.
How was Amandeep feeling when she said she couldn't find anything?
She felt overwhelmed and flustered, with too many rules to remember on a busy day.
What would you change first in Amandeep's plan?
Cut it down to three or four rules for the most common problems, short enough to remember without looking at the pages.

messages.content:

Dear Jaya,
You asked how the new planning system is going. Honestly? Badly, and I've worked out why.
After that workshop, I wrote if-then rules for everything in my week. If a client emails after six, then reply next morning. If a meeting has no agenda, then decline it. If I get interrupted, then note it and continue. If the report is late, then... I stopped counting at thirty.
Yesterday was the product launch. The phone rang nonstop, three people needed approvals, and a client was angry about an invoice. I didn't remember a single rule. I didn't even open the document. I just answered whatever was loudest, all day, like I always did.
Thirty rules is not a plan, it's a book. Nobody reads a book in a crisis.
I'm going to cut it down. Will tell you how.
Ishita

But meetings ran all afternoon that fortnight, and by Thursday the lunch rule had been ignored four days in a row. She noticed it and did not scold herself. Lunch always ended with a call rolling straight in. But at four she always shut her laptop. So on Friday she rewrote the rule: if I close my laptop at four, then I write down tomorrow's top task. Uday, at the next desk, saw the new sticky note and raised an eyebrow. "Same rule, different trigger," she said. On Monday the task was already written.

If a new request comes in, then ask for the deadline before saying yes.
If a meeting has no agenda, then ask for one.

On Friday she looked at the card and thought about when her day really slowed down. It was four o'clock, when the calls ended and she shut her laptop to stretch.

The next week, she cleared the inbox four days out of five.

Sami stood by the kitchen tap holding a small glass of water. Her big brother Emil waited at the table with bread, and Papa stood at the sink, ready to help. Sami looked at the glass, then at the table across the room.

Swati here. I sat next to Devang on Thursday before our seminar. He was glowing. "I can see it," he said, eyes shut. "The slides, the pause, everyone clapping, Yamini ma'am nodding." He had pictured it every night that week. He never opened his slides on another laptop and never checked the cable. When his turn came, the projector showed only a blue screen. He froze with the pen drive in his hand, said, "It worked yesterday," and stood there for a full minute. Yamini ma'am asked whether he could talk without slides. He shook his head. I don't know what was in his mind. He only looked like someone who had never once pictured this.

What did the projector show when Devang's turn came?
The projector showed only a blue screen.
What might Devang have been feeling as he stood there after saying "It worked yesterday"?
Devang was probably shocked and panicked, and perhaps embarrassed, since he froze for a full minute, though Swati cannot be sure.
What could Devang have practised beforehand?
Devang could have rehearsed a fallback, such as carrying a printed copy of the slides or practising the main points aloud without a screen.
How might Yamini have felt when Devang shook his head?
Yamini may have felt concerned for Devang, wanting to help but seeing the talk could not go on as planned.

Sunday night. Mridul lay on his hostel bed and pictured Tuesday's presentation on water harvesting. He walks in. Slides flow. The professor nods. Classmates clap at the end. He replayed it three times and fell asleep smiling.
His roommate Yusuf asked on Monday, "Did you practise?"

"What if the projector acts up? It did in my class last week."
"It won't," Mridul said.
Tuesday. The projector showed a blue screen. The technician took ten minutes. Mridul stood at the front with no printout and no notes, trying to remember what was on slide four. He skipped half his points, lost the order, and finished early. The professor wrote something in her notebook without looking up.
That evening he told Yusuf, "I imagined everything except the part that went wrong."

How long did the technician take?
The technician took ten minutes.

He felt panicked and lost, trying to remember slide four and skipping half his points.
What would you change first in how Mridul prepared?
Rehearse aloud at least once, and imagine the projector failing, then carry a printout or notes as a backup.
How might Yusuf see what happened on Tuesday?
Yusuf may feel sorry for Mridul but not surprised, since Yusuf had warned Mridul about the projector.

Arnab, you keep saying you've got the seminar "all in your head". Let your Ujjwal Chacha tell you about my final-year viva.
The night before, I lay in bed and played it like a film. I walk in, the examiners smile, my slides are beautiful, they ask easy questions, I answer brilliantly, they shake my hand. I watched that film maybe ten times. I felt completely ready.
I never once asked, what if something goes wrong?
Next morning, the power went off in the whole block. No projector. The examiners said, "Just explain it on the board."
I had never practised without slides. I couldn't remember the order of my own chapters. I drew one diagram wrong. I got a pass, but only just, and I walked out shaking.
That film in my head made me feel ready, beta. It just didn't make me ready.

The examiners said, "Just explain it on the board."

Ujjwal felt shaken and embarrassed, having scraped a pass after feeling completely ready the night before.

For the first, I keep the slides on paper in my bag. For the second, I wrote a short answer on a card: what the number includes, and what I will check and send by evening. The village school's cricket ground was still green from last week's rain when Siddharth sat on the wall with his notebook. The match against the next village was fixed for Sunday. "What if it rains?" he said aloud to Nitin, who was tying the stumps together. "Then the ground is mud and we have called sixty people for nothing." He tapped his pen. "Plan B. I ask the headmaster for the verandah, carrom and kabaddi indoors, or he keeps next Sunday free for us." Nitin shrugged. "Rain isn't in your hands." "No, but the day can be," said Siddharth. He wrote both options down and walked to the headmaster's office before evening. By the time the sun went down, next Sunday was in the ground register with the school's stamp.

Siddharth worried that the ground would be mud and sixty people would have been called for nothing.

Zeynep was in charge of the Year 10 cricket match against the school across town in Nairobi. Two weeks before, she looked at the fixture sheet and asked herself, what if it rains?
The long rains had started early. If the match was washed out, both teams would go home and the season would end without it.
So she wrote Plan B underneath. First, she asked the PE office if the indoor hall was free on the same afternoon. It was, from two to five. An indoor six-a-side game with a tennis ball would do. Second, she asked both coaches to hold the following Saturday as a reserve date.
Her teammate Abebe laughed. "You planned a match that hasn't even been rained on yet."
On the day, it poured at one. By two, both teams were in the hall, playing six-a-side. Nobody went home.

It was free from two to five.
What was Zeynep worried about two weeks before the match?
She was worried the long rains would wash out the match and the season would end without it being played.
What else could Zeynep add to the plan, and why?
She could tell both teams about Plan B in advance, so everyone knows where to go if it rains.

Abebe, who laughed at first, may be grateful and impressed when the rain comes and nobody has to go home.
