In the sports room of the Bhopal girls' school, Afreen pinned the notice for Saturday's inter-house cricket match. Then she stood back and frowned at the sky through the window.
"What if it rains?" she said to Sudha Ma'am, the games teacher. "It's July. If it's washed out, the final gets cancelled and the Class 12 girls never get to play before they leave."
Sudha Ma'am raised her eyebrows. "So what's your plan?"
Afreen took out her notebook. "Plan A: ground at nine. Plan B: if it's raining at eight, we move to the indoor hall and play tennis-ball cricket, six a side. Plan C: if the hall's taken, we use next Saturday. Can you book both?"
Ma'am booked the hall and wrote next Saturday in the register.
It drizzled at eight. By nine, both houses were in the hall, cheering.

They move to the indoor hall and play tennis-ball cricket, six a side.

Sit, Vaibhav. You want to know why I always carry two tickets? Let me tell you what Yash did at twenty. December, a banking exam in Lucknow, and every newspaper full of fog. My friends laughed. The train was five hours late. Half the platform sat on their bags staring at the empty tracks. I opened my folder, walked to the bus stand and caught the last bus. Bidisha's entrance exam was at ten on Sunday in Lucknow, and she had a seat on the night train from Kolkata. It was December. Her roommate Sabina had been stuck on the same line for six hours last winter because of fog.

If the train was running more than three hours late at Varanasi, she'd get off and take the 3.30 bus, which reached Lucknow at eight. She booked the bus seat, refundable, and wrote the timings on a card in her wallet.
At Varanasi, the train was running four hours late in thick fog. Bidisha got off, walked to the bus stand with her bag and took the 3.30 bus.
She reached the exam centre at nine.

The 3.30 bus reached Lucknow at eight.

Because at two in the morning in fog she didn't have to think or panic; she just followed the rule she had set.

Sabina may feel relieved and glad that her warning about the fog helped.

Trisha was organising the craft fair for women weavers in Mahuva, a small town near the coast, and she had booked the big community hall, which held two hundred. But last year only forty people had come, and the empty hall had felt sad.
This time, three weeks before, she sat in the panchayat office with her friend Bidisha and wrote a rule. "If fewer than sixty weavers and buyers confirm by Friday at six, we move to the smaller school hall." She told the school headmaster the same day, and he agreed to keep it free.
"Why decide now?" Bidisha asked.
"Because on the day I'll be panicking and want to hope for the best," Trisha said.
On Friday at six, the count was fifty-one. Trisha didn't argue with herself. She called the school and the community hall, and sent a message to all fifty-one: new venue, same time.
The school hall was full and lively.

How many confirmations were there on Friday at six?
The count was fifty-one.
Why did Trisha want to set the rule three weeks early?
She worried she would panic on the day and just hope for the best, so she wanted the decision made calmly in advance.
What else could Trisha set a trigger for, and why?
She could set a rule for bad weather, such as moving stalls indoors if rain is forecast, so another choice isn't made in a rush.
How might the weavers experience the smaller hall?
They may feel more encouraged, since a full, lively hall feels better than the sad, empty one of last year.

Ulla was organising the neighbourhood winter supper in Aarhus. The big church hall seated a hundred and twenty and cost four times as much as the library's meeting room, which seated seventy.
Her friend Dalia said, "Just book the big one. People always come."
"Last year they didn't," Ulla said. "Half the tables were empty." She opened her laptop. "So here's the rule. If fewer than sixty people have signed up by Friday noon, we move to the library room. If it's sixty or more, we keep the hall."
She told the library to hold the room until Friday afternoon and wrote the rule at the top of the sign-up sheet so the volunteers knew too.
Friday at noon, the sheet showed fifty-four names. Ulla sent one email: "We'll be cosy this year. Library, 6 p.m."
Dalia replied with a thumbs up. That evening, the library room was warm and full.

The sheet showed fifty-four names.

She probably felt calm and settled, because the decision was already made by her rule.

She could set a second rule, such as a waiting list over seventy, so the small room doesn't get overcrowded.

'Here it is,' Reena said, sliding a folder across the table. 'Twelve risks, twelve backup plans.'

'Even the one where the hall floods?' Kishore asked.

I'm Keerthana, and last year I led the move of our NGO's records to a new online system. I was determined nothing would catch us off guard.
So I wrote backup plans. What if the internet fails. What if the vendor shuts down. What if a volunteer deletes a file. What if there's a flood in the office. What if the software has a virus. Twelve risks, each with a two-page plan. My colleague Charu said, "Most of these won't happen." I said, better safe.
It took me three weeks. I felt very prepared.
What I hadn't done was the actual work. I hadn't cleaned the old data, trained the six volunteers, or tested the import even once.
On migration day, half the records came in with broken dates. Nobody knew how to fix them. None of my twelve plans covered it, because it wasn't a disaster. It was just the main job, not done.

How many risks did Keerthana write plans for?
Twelve risks, each with a two-page plan.
How did Keerthana feel after three weeks of writing backup plans?
Keerthana felt very prepared and confident, which made the failure on migration day more of a shock.
What would you change first in Keerthana's approach?
Spend most of the time on the main path, cleaning data, training volunteers and a test import, and write backups only for the two or three most likely risks.
How might Charu see migration day?
Charu may feel frustrated and a little vindicated, having warned that most of the risks wouldn't happen.

Supervisor's note, project review, 18 October
Mehak joined as project lead for the clinic booking system in August. She is careful and hardworking. Today's review showed what that can cost.
Her risk file is impressive: fourteen contingency plans, from server failure to a monsoon flooding the data centre to a vendor going bankrupt. Each has a flowchart. Baljeet, the developer on her team, told me she had spent most of September on them.
But the main path is behind. The appointment screen has not been tested with real clinic staff. The training guide is half written. Go-live is in eleven days.
When I asked about the testing, she looked stricken and said, "I thought if I covered every risk, the rest would be fine."
We agreed on a plan: freeze the contingency work, keep only the top three risks, and spend next week on testing and the training guide. I will check in on Friday.

How many contingency plans are in Mehak's risk file?
Fourteen contingency plans.
How did Mehak feel when asked about the testing?
She looked stricken, showing she was shocked and worried that the main work had been left behind.
Which approach would have suited Mehak better from the start?
Plan for the few likely and costly risks, then put most effort into testing and training on the main path.
How might the clinic staff be affected if go-live happened as things stand?
They might get a booking screen that was never tested with them and no finished training guide, which could make their work harder.

Vandana: Last year you told us you had twelve backup plans. What now?

Sangeeta: Three. I asked which risks are both likely and expensive if they happen: the supplier slipping, our lead developer being out, and the client changing scope. Each has a trigger. If the supplier's parts aren't here by the fifth, we order from the second supplier. If the developer is out two days running, we bring in the contractor.

The trigger is the supplier's parts not being there by the fifth.

Sangeeta wanted a list short enough to read and use, since a long one tends to be ignored.

Sangeeta could add it with a clear trigger and drop or merge the weakest of the others, so that the list stays short.

Panel delivery late: if the truck isn't dispatched by the 10th, then call the second supplier. School exams: if the exam dates are announced, then no drilling during them.
After each stage, he pulled the list out again. After the panels were delivered, he crossed off the delivery line. After exams ended, that one went too.

Tanuja drew five circles for the children. Then she made twenty-three dots for the laddoos and began putting one dot into each circle, round and round, crossing off dots as she went. After four rounds every circle held four dots. Three dots stood alone in the middle.

"Three left!" she said, and wrote the answer under her picture. Arnab looked, nodded and went on with his bucket.

How many laddoos were shared, and among how many children?
Twenty-three laddoos were shared equally among five children.
How was Tanuja feeling before she drew the picture?
Tanuja was confused and stuck, since the numbers swam in her head.
How could Tanuja check her answer?

How might Arnab see Tanuja's drawing?

Selin was stuck on her maths homework at the kitchen table in their Izmir flat. "Fourteen sweets shared equally among four children. How many does each get, and how many are left?"
Her friend Yara, who lived upstairs, was eating a biscuit. "Just divide."
"I can't see it in my head," Selin said.
She took a pencil and drew four big circles at the top of the page: four children. Then she drew fourteen dots along the bottom: sweets. One by one, she moved a dot into each circle, crossing it out at the bottom. One round. Two rounds. Three rounds.
Now each circle had three dots. At the bottom, two dots were still not crossed out.
"Three each," Selin said, tapping the circles. "And two left over!"
Yara leaned over. "Oh. That's easier than dividing."

She drew four big circles.
How did Selin feel when she saw the two leftover dots?
She felt excited and pleased, tapping the circles as the answer became clear.
What else could Selin do to check her answer?
She could multiply three by four and add the two left over, to see that it makes fourteen.
How might Yara see Selin's drawing?
Yara is surprised and thinks it looks easier than dividing, so she may try drawing next time.

In the Class 4 room at the government school in Moradabad, Varun Sir wrote a sum on the board. "Seventeen laddoos, five children, share equally. How many each? How many left?"

So she drew five smiling faces in her rough notebook, and seventeen small dots below. She gave one dot to each face, drawing a line from dot to face. Another round. A third.
She counted. Each face had three dots. Two dots at the bottom had no lines.
She put up her hand. "Three each, Sir. Two left over."
Varun Sir looked at her page. "Can you show everyone how you did it?"
Zeenat blushed, but she carried her notebook to the front.

I'm Neelam, and I share a lab with Zubin in the sociology department. Last Tuesday I watched him get unstuck.
He'd been writing his thesis outline as a list for weeks: Chapter 1, Chapter 2, and so on, with sources under each. He kept saying it felt messy but he couldn't see why.
That afternoon he took a big sheet of chart paper and drew boxes instead. Chapters in one colour, data sources in another, research questions in a third. Then he drew arrows from each chapter to whatever it needed.
Halfway through, he stopped. Two arrows, from Chapter 3 and Chapter 5, pointed to the same box: the migrant workers' survey.
"They both need the survey," he said out loud. "If the survey is late, two chapters fall."
He circled that box twice in red. The next morning, he emailed his guide asking to start the survey a month early.

Which box did two arrows point to?
The migrant workers' survey.
What might Zubin's saying it out loud suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he felt surprised and a bit alarmed, suddenly seeing the risk the list had hidden, though Neelam can only guess.
What else could Zubin do with the map now?
He could look for other boxes with many arrows, since those are the parts where a delay would cause the most harm.
How might Zubin's guide see the email asking to start early?
The guide may be pleased, seeing that Zubin has spotted a key risk and is planning ahead.

Hansa had wanted to start a weekend pottery class for children for over a year. Her flat in Ahmedabad had a small balcony, and she only had Sundays free from her bank job.

"Soon. I'm still planning the lessons for weeks nine to twelve."
"Have you called the clay supplier?"

By September, the notebooks were thicker. She still hadn't ordered clay, cleared the balcony or told a single parent.

1. One row per respondent. Delete the 14 test entries from the first day (they're marked TEST).
2. Ages as plain numbers, so "19 yrs" becomes 19.
3. Blank answers stay blank. Please don't fill them with zero.
4. Keep the raw file untouched and work on a copy.

Could you send me the first 30 cleaned rows by Wednesday at 6 pm? I'll look at them that evening, and if the format is right you can carry on with the rest at your own pace until the Sunday deadline. If anything in the raw file confuses you, message me before guessing. I'd much rather answer five small questions than fix one big surprise.

Thanks,
Lokesh

How many test entries does Wasim need to delete?
14 test entries from the first day, marked TEST.
What does the line 'message me before guessing' suggest Lokesh is worried about?
Lokesh is worried about quiet guesses turning into big mistakes later, and wants Wasim to feel free to ask rather than anxious about bothering anyone.
What else could Lokesh add to make the handover even clearer?
Attaching one already cleaned example row would show the format at a glance, so Wasim has less to interpret.
How might the email feel to Wasim?
Wasim probably feels trusted and clear about what 'done' means, with a safe check on Wednesday to catch errors before the Sunday deadline.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hands over a task with clear expectations and a check-in time [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

So, I'm Tushar, and last term I finally learnt how to hand work over properly. Our civil engineering group had traffic counts from four junctions, typed by four different people. Total mess. Indu offered to clean it. Earlier I'd have said "just sort it", then lain awake wondering what she was doing. This time I sat with her for ten minutes. I showed her exactly what I needed: times in 24-hour format, one junction per tab, and vehicle types spelt the same way every time, "two-wheeler", never "bike" or "scooty". Then I said, "Don't spend more than an hour before you show me. Send me Junction B by Wednesday lunch." She sent it Wednesday at noon, and there was one problem: she'd merged buses and vans. We fixed it in five minutes, not five days.

Which junction did Indu send first, and when?
Junction B, on Wednesday at noon.
How did Tushar feel about handing over work in the past?
Tushar felt anxious and out of control, lying awake wondering what the other person was doing after just saying "just sort it".
What would you change first if the group had missed the Wednesday check?
Set a new short check straight away on one small piece, so a mistake like merging buses and vans is still caught early.
What is it like for Indu to get such clear instructions?
Indu can work confidently without guessing, and the early check means her one mistake was cheap to fix rather than embarrassing at the end.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hands over a task with clear expectations and a check-in time [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Vasudha had been made team lead at the cooperative office in the small town only a month before. On Monday she handed the monthly collections report to Yamini. "Do it the way you think best."

On Thursday Yamini brought it: tidy tables and a short summary. Vasudha read two pages, frowned and said, "I'll just fix a few things." By night she had rewritten every table in her own layout and swapped out the summary. On Friday morning Yamini opened the file and saw none of her own words. She said nothing, put her pen down and went to check the ledger, quieter than usual.

The next month, when Vasudha asked who could take the report, the room went still. She stayed until eight, doing all of it herself.

What did Vasudha do after reading two pages of the report?
Vasudha said she would just fix a few things, and then rewrote every table.
How might Yamini have felt on seeing none of her own words in the file?
Yamini probably felt distrusted and discouraged, shown by saying nothing and going quiet.
What could Vasudha do instead of rewriting the whole report?
Vasudha could say clearly what the report needs before it starts, then comment on one or two specific points and let Yamini make the changes.
Why might the team go quiet when Vasudha asks who can take the report?
They may fear that their work will simply be redone, so nobody wants to put in the effort.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hands off work but keeps redoing it because it is not done her way [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Aiko had been team lead at the Rotterdam shipping office for three weeks when she handed Emil the quarterly supplier report. "Take it end to end," she said. "I trust you." On Thursday evening his draft arrived. It was solid, just ordered differently from how she would have done it. At eleven that night she was still at her kitchen table, moving every section, changing his charts, rewording his summary. She sent the new version to the client at 8 a.m. with her name first. At stand-up, Emil scrolled through the file history and went quiet. He didn't offer to take the next report. By Friday Aiko had two reports of her own on her desk, a stiff neck, and a colleague who answered her in single words.

What time was Aiko still working on the report?
At eleven that night she was still at her kitchen table.
What does Emil going quiet at stand-up suggest about how he felt?
He likely felt hurt and distrusted: his solid draft had been rewritten without a word to him, despite "I trust you".
What could Aiko do differently with the next report?
She could agree up front on the structure she wants, then give Emil notes to fix his own draft instead of rewriting it.
How does the situation look from the client's side?
The client only sees one report, but if Emil pulls back, the team slows down and Aiko becomes a bottleneck for every future piece.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hands off work but keeps redoing it because it is not done her way [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the community centre, Aadhya had been programme lead for a month. The grant progress report was due in ten days, so she asked Anirban to draft it; he had run the evening classes all year and knew the numbers. His draft landed on Tuesday. It told the story through two learners, where Aadhya would have used tables. That weekend she rewrote it from the first line. On Monday Anirban opened the shared folder, saw his name gone from the file, and closed the laptop without a word. After that he stopped suggesting ideas in meetings. Meanwhile Aadhya's own budget sheet, the thing only she could do, slid past its deadline. The funder got a neat report. The centre got a quieter Anirban and a lead running on four hours' sleep.

When did Anirban's draft arrive?
His draft landed on Tuesday.
What was Anirban feeling when he closed the laptop without a word?
He likely felt hurt and pushed aside, since his work and his name had been removed from the file.
Which approach would have suited Aadhya better?
Telling Anirban at the start that the funder likes tables, then letting him adjust his own draft, would keep his effort and her time.
How do the learners at the centre get affected by this?
With Anirban withdrawing and Aadhya exhausted, fewer new ideas reach the classes and planning slows.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hands off work but keeps redoing it because it is not done her way [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday. Anirban used to send colleagues step-by-step instructions. This time he told Sahil only the outcome. "I need a one-page guide that a new customer can follow in five minutes. How you build it is up to you." Sahil nodded slowly, surprised.

Wednesday. Anirban's fingers hovered over the chat window, ready to ask about progress. Instead he waited. Across the office, Sahil was drawing a flowchart with four boxes.

Friday. Sahil sent the guide. Anirban gave it to a tester from sales, who followed it in four minutes. "It works. One thing: the second box says onboarding. Can it say first login?" Sahil changed it in ten minutes. "Thanks for not telling me how," Sahil said.

How long should a new customer need to follow the guide?
A new customer should be able to follow it in five minutes.
How did Sahil feel when Anirban gave only the outcome?
Sahil felt surprised, and perhaps pleased to be trusted with the method.
What could Anirban do if the guide had failed the test?
Anirban could explain exactly where the tester got stuck and ask Sahil to revise it, keeping the choice of method with Sahil.
How might the tester from sales see the guide?
The tester would find it clear, since it took only four minutes to follow, and would be glad the test helped improve it.

metadata.subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Come, sit, Alka. You asked how your Damini Aunty learnt to run a team. I'll tell you. I was twenty-five, newly put in charge of the pharmacy night shift, and I checked every label the junior pharmacist printed. Every single one. By the third week I was falling asleep standing, and the junior had stopped asking me anything. One night I noticed the junior had spotted a wrong dose on a doctor's slip and said nothing, waiting for me to find it. That frightened me more than any mistake. The next evening I said, "Here is what a good shift looks like: every order checked against the chart, doubts flagged to me, the log complete by six." How to get there, I left to the junior. At the end of each week we looked at the log together. Within a month the log was cleaner than mine.

How old was Damini's younger self when put in charge of the night shift?
Twenty-five, newly put in charge of the pharmacy night shift.
Why was young Damini frightened on the night the junior stayed silent?
Seeing the junior spot a wrong dose and stay silent, waiting; it frightened the young lead because checking everything had taught the junior not to speak up.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Stating what a good shift looks like and leaving the method to the junior; clear standards plus weekly feedback built skill and trust instead of dependence.
How might the junior pharmacist have felt once the lead stopped rechecking every label?
Probably trusted and more responsible, which is why the junior's log soon became cleaner than the lead's.

metadata.subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Raghav had a problem: the client dashboard was due Friday, and he would be on a site visit in the hills all week with one bar of signal. On his last project he had hovered over Harish's shoulder, changing fonts and filters, and both of them had been miserable. This time there was no chance to hover. On Monday morning he wrote three lines on the whiteboard: "The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance. It must load in under five seconds. Numbers must match the finance sheet." He turned to Harish. "How you build it is up to you." On Thursday night, from a guesthouse, he opened Harish's link. It was not how he'd have done it; it was simpler. He sent two notes on the colour labels and one "This is really clear." The client signed off on Friday.

What three things did Raghav write on the whiteboard?
The client must see weekly sales by region at a glance, it must load in under five seconds, and the numbers must match the finance sheet.
How did Raghav feel when he saw Harish's version was not how he'd have done it?
Raghav may have felt a flicker of unease, but he felt reassured that it was simpler and met the goals, and chose to praise it rather than redo it.
What else could Raghav try if he had good signal and was tempted to hover again?
He could still fix a single midweek check-in instead of watching every step, so Harish keeps ownership of the method.
What is it like for Harish on this project compared with the last one?
Harish gets room to choose the method and clear, specific feedback, instead of constant changes, so the work feels his own.

metadata.subtype: Approach: agrees what good looks like, then steps back and gives feedback [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Mili sat on the floor with a plastic pot, pulling at its lid. It would not open. She grunted, pushed, and then gave a small whimper. She crawled to Mummy and held the pot up high.

"What have you got, Mili?"

"Ah! Ah!"

"Stuck? Let Mummy see." Mummy twisted the lid slowly, so Mili could watch the turn. "Pop!"

Mili patted the pot, then pushed it back into Mummy's hands. "Again!"

"Again? All right, close it."

What did Mili hold up to Mummy?
Mili held up the plastic pot.
What did Mili want when she whimpered?
Mili wanted the lid opened and needed help, since she could not manage it alone.
What could Mummy do to help Mili learn?
Mummy could twist the lid slowly and let Mili put her hands on it too.
How might Mummy feel when Mili brought the pot over?
Mummy might feel pleased that Mili came to ask for help instead of giving up.

metadata.subtype: Approach: brings a problem to a caregiver [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Note for the crèche, Tuesday

This morning Jyoti sat with her little jar of shape blocks and pulled at the lid until her face went red. Then she stopped, walked over, and pushed the jar into my lap with a small whimper: "Mama, Mama." I loosened it a little and handed it back so she could finish opening it herself. She did, and clapped 🙂 She may bring you stuck things today as well.

Vandana

What did Jyoti push into the writer's lap?
Her little jar of shape blocks, with a small whimper.
What was Jyoti feeling before she walked over to the writer?
She was frustrated: she pulled until her face went red before giving up and asking for help.
What does the writer's approach do well?
Loosening the lid a little and handing it back lets Jyoti finish the job herself, so she feels proud of her effort and also learns that asking helps.
How might a crèche teacher use this note during the day?
The teacher can expect Jyoti to bring stuck things over and can respond the same way, helping a little rather than doing it all.

metadata.subtype: Approach: brings a problem to a caregiver [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the courtyard, Amma sat sorting rice. Mahima, not yet two, had the little wooden box her big brother Divyansh had made her. The sliding lid was stuck. She pushed with both thumbs, then banged it on the floor. Her lip wobbled. She toddled over, leaned on Amma's knee and held the box up, whimpering. Amma eased the lid back a finger's width. Mahima slid it open and shook out three tamarind seeds.

What did Divyansh make for Mahima?
A small wooden box with a sliding lid.
How can you tell Mahima was upset before she went to Amma?
She banged the box and her lip wobbled; she was frustrated and close to tears when nothing worked.
What could Amma try next time to help Mahima learn?
She could show Mahima slowly how to push the lid sideways with her thumb, so next time Mahima might manage it alone.
How might Divyansh feel if he saw the lid stick?
He might feel a bit sorry that his gift was hard to open and want to sand the lid so it slides easily.

metadata.subtype: Approach: brings a problem to a caregiver [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Ojas sat on the shop step in the small town with one school shoe on and the other's laces hanging loose. He tried, twisted, and the laces slid apart. He sighed. "Dada, will you show me how to tie it?"

Dada put down the newspaper. "Watch slowly, beta. Cross. Tuck. Make a bunny ear."

Ojas watched, chin on his knees. Then Dada put his big hands over Ojas's small ones, and together they pulled the loops tight. "Now you."

Ojas stuck out his tongue and crossed the laces alone. The bow was lopsided, but it held. "I did it!"

What did Dada say to do?
Dada said to cross, tuck and make a bunny ear.
How did Ojas feel after tying the bow?
Ojas felt proud and happy, and called out "I did it!"
What could Ojas do to get better at tying the bow?
Ojas could practise a little each day with Dada nearby, and ask to be shown slowly again if he gets stuck.
How might Dada feel while showing Ojas?
Dada might feel patient and pleased to see Ojas learn.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks a trusted adult a direct question [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Xin's new trainers had real laces, like the ones his friend Yosef tied all by himself. At the door, Xin tugged the loops into a knot that fell apart twice. He sat on the step, then looked up. "Yeye, can you show me? Slowly?" Grandpa knelt down. "Watch. Bunny ear, then round the tree, then through the hole." He did it once, very slowly. Then he put his big warm hands over Xin's small ones and they made the bunny ear together. The first bow was lopsided. The second one held all the way to the park.

What did Xin ask Yeye?
"Yeye, can you show me? Slowly?"
Why did Xin want to learn to tie his laces?
He wanted to be like his friend Yosef, and he felt frustrated when his knot kept falling apart; he hoped Yeye's help would fix it.
What small step helped Xin most?
Grandpa's hands guiding his made the steps easy to feel; next time Xin could try alone while Grandpa just watches.
How might Yeye feel being asked for help?
Yeye probably felt pleased and patient, glad that Xin trusted him enough to ask.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks a trusted adult a direct question [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

After swimming class at the sports club, Ojas pulled on his school shoes and stared at the flapping laces. Tejas, from his class, was already out of the door. Ojas carried his shoe to the bench where Dadu waited. "Dadu, teach me the loops. Tejas can do it." Dadu set the shoe on his knee. "Look carefully." He made one loop, wrapped the other lace round it and pulled, very slowly. "Now you." It flopped open. Dadu covered Ojas's fingers with his own. "Together." Round, through, pull. Ojas grinned at the bow.

Where was Dadu waiting?
On the bench, where Ojas carried his shoe after swimming class.
What might Ojas be feeling when Tejas was already out of the door?
He probably felt a little left behind and embarrassed that he couldn't tie his laces yet, which pushed him to ask Dadu.
What would you advise Ojas's teacher at the club if other children need the same help?
Show the loops slowly once, then guide each child's hands, the same way Dadu did, before letting them try alone.
How does Dadu see Ojas's request?
Dadu seems happy to be asked and takes it seriously, slowing down so Ojas can actually learn.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks a trusted adult a direct question [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Abhinav here. I sit behind Manjula, so I saw everything. The problem said a rope is 12 metres long and is cut into pieces of 3 metres. How many pieces? Manjula worked on it for ten minutes, biting her pencil. Then she picked up her notebook and walked to the teacher's desk.

"I tried, Ma'am. I did 12 minus 3 and got 9. But 9 doesn't sound like pieces."

The teacher looked at her page. "What does 9 tell you?"

"It's the rope left after one cut. I have to keep cutting... oh! It's 12 shared into 3s." She wrote 4 and smiled. I don't know if she felt silly or happy, but she ran back to her seat fast.

What answer did Manjula get when she did 12 minus 3?
Manjula got 9.
How was Manjula feeling about her answer of 9, and how can you tell?
Manjula felt doubtful and unsure, since she said 9 did not sound like pieces, so she wanted help finding the mistake.
What could Manjula try next time she is stuck?
Manjula could draw the rope cut into pieces first, and bring her attempt to the teacher if she is still stuck.
Why can Abhinav only guess how Manjula felt at the end?
Abhinav sat behind and saw only the smile and the quick run back, so cannot know Manjula's feelings for sure.

metadata.subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: Avni spent twenty minutes on question 7, the one about two trains leaving from different stations. She tried drawing the tracks, rubbed it out, tried a table. Her eraser left a hole in the page. "Okay," she whispered. "I've tried three ways. Now I need someone to see what I did, not just give me the answer."

Tuesday: Before assembly she took her messy page to Reena Ma'am. "I think I went wrong somewhere here," Avni said, pointing. "I added their speeds, but maybe I should have subtracted?" Reena Ma'am smiled. "What made you unsure?" Avni thought. "They're going the same way, so they're not coming closer fast."

Thursday: In the quiz, a similar question came up. Avni didn't panic. She drew the arrows first.

Which question did Avni spend twenty minutes on?
Question 7, the one about two trains leaving from different stations.
How did Avni feel on Thursday when a similar question came up?
She felt calm and confident; she didn't panic because she now understood why the direction of the trains mattered.
Why did bringing her messy page to Reena Ma'am work well?
Reena Ma'am could see exactly where Avni's thinking went wrong and ask a question, so Avni found the fix herself.
What would change if Avni had only asked for the answer?
She might have copied it without knowing why, and the Thursday quiz question could have caught her out again.

metadata.subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Shreya, you think I was always good at sums? No. When I was a girl of eleven, there was a problem about filling a tank with two taps. I sat with it for a whole evening. I tried one way, then another. My pages were full of crossings. My brother said, "Just ask Master-ji for the answer." But I thought, if I only get the answer, I will be stuck again next week. So I took my crossed-out pages to school. I told Master-ji, "This is how I thought. Somewhere it breaks." He read my pages and put his finger on one line. "Here, you forgot one tap was emptying." I nearly laughed. The next tank problem, I solved alone. That's how your Pooja Nani learnt.

What was the problem young Pooja struggled with?
A problem about filling a tank with two taps.
Why did young Pooja refuse to just ask for the answer?
She was worried that with only the answer she would be stuck again next week; she wanted to understand where her own thinking broke.
What choice in the story made the difference, and why?
Taking her crossed-out pages to Master-ji; seeing her working let him point to the exact line where she forgot one tap was emptying.
How might Master-ji have felt reading her pages?
He was probably pleased and impressed to see a student who had really tried, which made it easy for him to help quickly.

metadata.subtype: Approach: seeks a teacher when stuck after trying alone [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: Thank you for Tuesday

Dear Pallavi,

Thank you for meeting me at the coffee counter. I came with three questions written on a card, and your answers were clear. First, skills: you said to get comfortable with spreadsheets and with writing short, clear updates. Second, entry paths: an internship in third year, or a junior analyst opening through campus placements. Third, daily work: mostly cleaning data in the mornings and meetings after lunch. I took notes on all of it, and next week I will compare them with what a second alumnus tells me. I have already signed up for a spreadsheet course. Thank you again for your time.

Best wishes,
Lokesh

What were the three questions about?
The three questions were about skills, entry paths and daily work.
How might Lokesh have felt going into the meeting with a card of written questions?
Lokesh probably felt keen but a little nervous, wanting to make good use of the time and get a clear picture for planning.
What could Lokesh do with the notes next?
Lokesh could compare them with the second alumnus's answers, see what matches, and choose a first step.
How might Pallavi have felt on receiving a student with prepared questions?
Pallavi may have felt pleased and respected, since the student took time to prepare.

metadata.subtype: Approach: prepares questions before meeting a professional [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Karthik, final year, and I want to tell you about the most useful coffee I ever had. I was stuck between physiotherapy and sports science, so I messaged an alumna, Vandana, who runs a clinic now. Before meeting her, I sat down and wrote exactly three questions. One: what skills matter most in her first two years? Two: which entry path would she pick today, the master's or a clinic job straight away? Three: what does a normal Tuesday look like for her? At the café I put my notebook on the table and wrote while she talked. She laughed and said most students just ask, "Is it a good career?" That evening I made two columns in my notebook and compared her answers with what my professor had told me.

How many questions did Karthik write before the meeting?
Exactly three questions.
How do you think Karthik felt going into the meeting?
Karthik likely felt a little nervous but prepared and focused, since the questions were written and ready in the notebook.
What else could Karthik do to get a fuller picture?
Speak to one more person on the other path, sports science, with the same three questions, so the comparison is fair.
How does Vandana see Karthik's approach?
She seems amused and pleased; she laughs because most students only ask "Is it a good career?"

metadata.subtype: Approach: prepares questions before meeting a professional [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

My name's Jatin. I share a room with Aadhya at the hostel, and I watched how she got ready to meet the alumnus who works as an urban planner. The night before, she wasn't scrolling. She was writing on an index card, crossing out, rewriting. When I peeked, I saw three questions: skills to learn now, how people actually get their first job, and what a working day is like. In the morning she ironed a kurta, then read the card again on the bus. When she came back she had two pages of notes, underlined in two colours. She didn't say much about how it went. She just pinned the pages above her desk, next to her placement list, and started marking things off.

Where did Aadhya write her questions?
On an index card, the night before.
What might Aadhya have been feeling, judging from the cues Jatin describes?
She seemed serious and perhaps a bit nervous, rewriting her card and reading it again on the bus; she also seems determined afterwards.
What could Aadhya try next time to get even more from such a meeting?
She could send her three questions ahead, so the alumnus can think about them and give fuller answers.
How might the alumnus see Aadhya's preparation?
The alumnus would likely feel respected and find it easier to help, because her questions were clear and specific.

metadata.subtype: Approach: prepares questions before meeting a professional [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Darshan here. I run the stall next to Anusha's at the weekend market, so I heard the whole thing. Farhan, an adviser from the city, told Anusha, "Double your price on the handmade candles. Premium sells." Anusha wrote it down and nodded at every line. I did not hear a single "why". The next Saturday, candles that sold at forty went up to eighty. Nobody bought. Farhan's customers in the city pay for the box and the fancy label; ours are neighbours who compare with the shop by the bus stand. By afternoon Anusha's table was still full and she was rearranging it for the third time. I don't know if Anusha blamed the advice or the customers. She only said, "He's the expert."

What did Farhan tell Anusha to do?
Farhan told Anusha to double the price on the handmade candles.
How might Anusha have felt as the candles did not sell?
Anusha probably felt worried and uncertain, but covered it by saying "He's the expert."
What could Anusha have asked Farhan before changing the price?
Anusha could have asked why he suggested it and whether it works in a small weekend market like hers, or tried the new price on only some candles.
How might customers at the market see the doubled price?
Customers might compare it with the shop by the bus stand and think it too much for a market stall.

metadata.subtype: Approach: treats an expert's view as final without asking the reasons [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Week 1: At the start-up meet, Irfan, a mentor who advises café owners in the big city, looked at Aparna's price list for her home-baked cakes. "Too cheap," he said. "Double everything. People pay for premium." Aparna nodded and wrote it down. She didn't ask why.

Week 3: She printed new cards with the doubled prices. Her regulars in the small town, mostly teachers and shop owners ordering for birthdays, went quiet. Only two orders came that week instead of the usual nine.

Week 5: A neighbour said gently, "Beta, we loved your cakes, but this is city money." Aparna sat with the order book and realised Irfan's clients were office crowds in the city, not her street. She had never asked what his advice was based on.

How many orders came in week 3, compared with usual?
Only two orders instead of the usual nine.
How did Aparna feel when she sat with the order book in week 5?
She probably felt dismayed and a bit foolish, realising she had followed Irfan's advice without asking what it was based on.
What could Aparna have asked Irfan in week 1?
She could have asked why he suggested doubling, and who his clients were, then tested one new price with a few regulars before changing everything.
How did the change look to Aparna's regular customers?
To her regulars it felt like the cakes were suddenly priced for the city, not for them, so they quietly stopped ordering.

metadata.subtype: Approach: treats an expert's view as final without asking the reasons [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-five, before this workshop had a sign board. I made hand-stitched cushion covers, and I found an adviser, Francis, who had helped big wholesale sellers. He said, "Cut your price in half. Win on volume." He sounded so sure, and I was so eager, I didn't ask a single question. I cut my prices. But my buyers were small boutiques. They saw the new price and thought the quality had dropped. Two stopped ordering. One owner told me, "At that price, it can't be handwork." Francis wasn't wrong for his world. His world was different from mine. Remember that, when you start: Binita Aunty learnt it the costly way.

What did Francis tell young Binita to do?
"Cut your price in half. Win on volume."
Why didn't young Binita question Francis's advice?
She was eager and he sounded so sure, so she felt too impressed and hurried to ask why.
At what point in the story could Binita have made a better choice?
When Francis gave the advice; asking what kind of sellers he had helped would have shown his wholesale world differed from her boutique buyers.
How did the boutique owners see the lower prices?
They took the cheaper price as a sign the quality had dropped, and one said it couldn't be handwork at that price.

metadata.subtype: Approach: treats an expert's view as final without asking the reasons [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

This time I asked, "Why?" She explained that in the big city people will not order without it, and the cost gets spread over many orders. That made sense for her city, but my town has one main road. The project night at Vasudha's house was the first time I really thought about why my parents said no. I'm Yusuf. We had a model to finish and then a film, which meant leaving around eleven. Abbu said, "Beta, no. Back by nine." I nearly argued, the way I always did. Instead I lay on my bed and thought: what is he actually scared of? It wasn't Vasudha, he knew her family. It wasn't the film. It was the auto ride back through the market after dark. So I went to him and said, "What if my cousin brings me back on his bike? He works late near there anyway." Abbu thought about it. "Call him first, then ask me again." My cousin said yes. I stayed till eleven.

Back by nine.

'Before anyone gets annoyed,' Parul said, putting three sheets on the table, 'I made options.'

'Options for what?' asked Kishore.

'The chores. Option one: a weekly rota, one job each. Option two: swap jobs every month. Option three: pay a helper for the bathroom and split the cost.'

'That last one feels expensive.'

'Then we drop it. I can live with the first two, but not with everyone doing what they feel like.'

Kishore laughed. 'So the fallback is a rota?'

'Yes. If we can't agree on the swap, we start the rota on Monday.'

'Rota's fine,' called their third flatmate from the sofa.

'Fine,' said Kishore. 'Rota with a monthly swap?'

'Deal.'

How many options had Parul written down?
Parul made three options.
How does Parul seem to feel going into the talk, and how can you tell?
Parul seems calm and prepared, since Parul offered options, knew what was acceptable and did not argue when one was rejected.
What could Parul do if the roommates reject all three options?
Parul could ask what each roommate finds hard about chores and shape a fourth option together.

Kishore may feel relaxed and respected, since the choices were laid out and the objection to the costly one was accepted.

"Stop," said Madhuri. "Let me ask something else. What matters most to you in this deal?"

Arnab rubbed his forehead. "Honestly? Cash by Friday. My cloth supplier wants payment then, and I'm short."

"If I pay half now and half on delivery, can you come down on the price?"

They shook hands. The bags were packed on Thursday, and both were relieved.

In the university admissions office, Swati had kept two email slots a day, eleven and four, for a month. The rest of the time she worked on the scholarship files that needed long quiet reading. It worked, until last Tuesday, when a student's visa letter sat unread from noon until four and the student missed an embassy slot. Swati felt terrible. She didn't scrap the slots. Instead she printed a small card and stuck it on the office door and in her email signature: "For urgent student issues, call the desk phone, extension 214." She told Farida, who sat at the front desk, "If anyone says urgent, put them through. I'd rather be interrupted than let that happen again." On Friday the desk phone rang once. Everything else waited till four.

What extension did Swati put on the card?
Extension 214, the desk phone.
How did Swati feel after the student missed the embassy slot?
She felt terrible and responsible, which pushed her to find a fix without giving up her quiet reading time.
What made Swati's change better than dropping the email slots?
It kept her focus time for the scholarship files but gave a quick route for real emergencies, so nothing urgent waits for hours.
How might Farida see her new role in this?
Farida may feel trusted to judge what's urgent and put people through, which makes the front desk more useful.

Subject: New way to reach me

Hi Simran and team,

Quick update. You know I've been checking email only at 10 and 3 so I can do the planning work properly. Most of you have said it's been fine. But last week Simran's message about the caterer cancelling sat in my inbox for four hours, and she had to handle it alone. That wasn't fair on her.

So I'm keeping the two slots, because they really help. But from today, if anything is urgent, a vendor dropping out, a client on the phone, someone unwell, please call my mobile; the number is in my signature. I'll pick up even in focus time. Everything else can wait for 10 or 3.

Thanks for putting up with my experiments 🙂

Reena

Only at 10 and 3.

Reena feels guilty and a bit uneasy, saying it wasn't fair on Simran.

A few examples of what isn't urgent, so the team knows when a call is right and when to wait for the slot.

Anjali, come, I will tell you about the time Dorje bragged. I was fifteen, and I had started a coding tutorial three times and quit three times. One Sunday, half joking, I typed into our class group: "I will finish the whole coding tutorial in thirty days." Thumbs-ups came back, and one boy wrote, "Let's see." My ears went hot. I did not want to look foolish. So I took a pencil and drew a chart on the door: one hour every evening after dinner, seven to eight. On the lazy days, the chart and the group were both staring at me. I finished on day twenty-nine. I still think about how the promise pushed me on the tired days.

Dorje promised thirty days.

Dorje felt embarrassed and did not want to look foolish.

Drawing a chart for one hour every evening, seven to eight, turned the promise into a daily routine.

Divyansh typed it into his class group before he could chicken out: "I'm finishing the web design tutorial in 30 days. You can check." Twelve thumbs came back, and one "sure bro 😏". That stung. Now he had to do it. The problem was the laptop: his sister Deepika needed it every evening for her college work, and the power went off at least twice a week. So he set a rule. One hour every morning, six to seven, before anyone else woke up. He charged the laptop the night before in case of cuts, and kept a notebook to tick each day. On day nine the power went at six-twenty; he read the lesson notes on his phone instead. On day thirty he posted a link to his first web page.

One hour every morning, six to seven.

He felt embarrassed that someone doubted him, and didn't want to look foolish in front of the class.

Find another fixed hour when the laptop is free, and keep ticking the notebook so the promise stays visible.

In the school coding club group, Anirban posted a challenge: "Who can build a small game in a month?" Varun, who usually lurked, surprised himself by replying, "Me. By the 30th. Watch." Anirban pinned the message. Walking home past the vegetable market, Varun's stomach turned. Now everyone would see if he quit. That night he stuck a paper calendar above his desk in the flat and wrote: 7 to 8 pm, game tutorial, every day. He told his mother not to call him for dinner before eight. Some nights he did only one tiny lesson. He crossed off every day anyway. On the 28th he shared a jumpy little frog game in the club group. Anirban replied first: "Told you you'd do it."

Three days before the first paper, Nihal opened his phone and looked at the racing game he played every night. He pressed and held the icon, and deleted it. Then, before lights out, he unplugged his charger and walked to Parth's bed.

"Keep this till seven."

"Seriously?" said Parth. "Your phone is at eleven percent. It'll die by midnight."

"That's the plan."

The first night Nihal lay awake wanting to check something, anything. The second night he read organic chemistry until sleep came. On the morning of the paper he collected his charger, and his phone showed forty-four unread messages that could wait.

Nihal gave the charger to Parth.

Two weeks before semester exams, Vishal looked at the screen-time report on his phone: five hours a day, mostly one racing game. His classmate Nazia, sitting next to him in the canteen, whistled. "That's a part-time job." Back in his room at the hostel in Bengaluru, Vishal did two things. He deleted the game, not just logged out. Then he handed his charger to his roommate, Abhay. "Keep this at night. Give it back at seven in the morning, even if I beg." Abhay grinned and tucked it into his own drawer. The first night Vishal reached for his phone at eleven, saw the battery at 12 percent, sighed and opened his circuits notes instead. By the end of the week his notes were finally complete.

How many hours a day was Vishal spending on his phone?
Five hours a day, mostly one racing game.

He felt tempted and a little frustrated, sighing when he saw the low battery, before turning to his notes.

"Akash, can you do me a strange favour?"
"Depends."
"Take my charger every night at ten. Give it back after breakfast."
"Why?"
Pradeep held up his phone. "I just deleted the video game. But if the phone's charged, I'll find something else. Exams start in twelve days."
"You deleted it? The one you've been playing since first year?"
"Gone. I'll reinstall it after the last paper."
"And if you ask me for the charger at midnight?"
"Say no. Even if I say it's urgent."
Akash laughed and held out his hand. "Fine. I'm keeping it in my cupboard."
That night, at eleven, Pradeep picked up his phone out of habit. Eight percent. He put it down and opened his notes.
"Good choice," Akash said from his bed, without looking up.

When does Pradeep ask Akash to return the charger?
After breakfast.
What does Pradeep's 'Say no, even if I say it's urgent' suggest about how he feels?
He is worried about his own weak moments and wants a firm guard, knowing he'll be tempted.

Aparna here. Harsha, who sits opposite me at the design studio, told me over lunch what he had done. "I paid for three months at the gym, all at once," he said. "I know myself. If I pay month to month, I'll skip and tell myself I'll pay next time. But money already gone will make me feel silly for not going." He said it like a rule he had checked. The first week I saw his gym bag under the desk every morning. On day nine it stayed on the chair and he left at six sharp. I don't know if he enjoys it or just doesn't want to waste the money. When I asked, he shrugged and said, "Either is fine with me."

How many months did Harsha pay for?
Harsha paid for three months, all at once.
What did Harsha expect from paying everything at once?
Harsha expected that money already gone would make him feel silly for skipping, so he would go.

"Last year I paid monthly and quit in week three, because stopping cost me nothing. If I pay for three months now, skipping means wasting money I already spent. I hate wasting money." He paid for three months. His friend Tanvir raised an eyebrow.

Week 5: Rain, a late night at work, and a strong urge to skip. Hrithik looked at the receipt on his fridge. "Already paid for this morning." He went, grumbling.

Week 12: Tanvir asked if he'd renew. Hrithik shrugged. "Maybe monthly now. Going is just what I do in the morning."

The receipt for the three-month plan.

Siami, you asked how I kept at the gym all these years. When I was twenty-four and new at the post office in Aizawl, I tried three times and quit three times. Each time I paid by the month, and each time the first bad weather stopped me. So I sat down and thought: what will stop your Lokesh Uncle from quitting? I knew myself. I hate losing money more than I hate cold mornings. So I paid for three whole months, all at once, and told my friends. On the wet, grey mornings, I lay in bed and thought, "That money is already gone. If you stay here, you're throwing it away." And up I got. After three months, I didn't need the trick.

Friday, 9:30 pm. Well, that plan is dead. On Monday I set a blocker to lock every app on my phone, all day, no exceptions. No messages, no maps, no bank. I thought: cold turkey, total focus. Today at eleven, Ishita sent a photo of the client's signed form on the work chat and asked me to forward it within ten minutes. My phone would not open the chat. I hunted for a way round it, panicked, deleted the blocker altogether, and still sent the form twenty minutes late. Now everything is open again and I scrolled for an hour tonight. The rule was too strict. It never made room for the one app I actually need.

Naveen

Arnab ran the accounts for a small seed shop in the market town of Bolpur. After weeks of losing evenings to his phone, he installed a strict blocker on Monday morning: every app locked until 9 pm. He felt proud as he slid the phone into his pocket. At noon a farmer came to pay for seed bags and wanted to pay through the phone. Himani, the owner, called out, "Arnab, check if the money's come." He couldn't open anything. The farmer waited, frowning. Arnab fumbled with the blocker's settings, deleted it in a panic and finally checked. That night he didn't reinstall it. "It's useless," he told Himani. "Too much trouble." His evenings went back to scrolling.

Until 9 pm.

Blocking games at night: that had helped; he'd slept better. The daytime block on work chat: that had hurt. So he set a new rule. Games blocked for four hours before each shift and during it, work apps always open. His teammate Bhupen, who had watched the first attempt collapse, asked, "Still locked out of everything?" In his flat in Gurugram, Mohit reopened the blocker app he had deleted a week ago in a panic. His colleague Afreen, visiting to work on their joint presentation, peered at the screen. "Round two?" "Round two, smarter." He talked it through as he set it up. "Last time I blocked everything all day. Work chat, email, maps, even the bank. Of course I broke it by noon." He tapped the settings. "What actually helped was evenings without games. I finished two books that week." So he set it: games and video apps blocked from eight to eleven every night; work apps never blocked. Afreen nodded. In the school hostel study hall, Akash sat with his phone, thinking about a lazy evening. Then he remembered: seven o'clock, call with Usha. Yesterday they had agreed that both would be on a call, cameras off, each would say a target, and then they would work for forty minutes. "If I'm late, Usha waits, and I'll feel bad," he whispered to himself. He opened the physics book at five to seven. At seven Usha's voice came: "Ready? I'm doing two history chapters." Dear Shreya Didi,

You asked how my studying is going this term. Honestly, better than ever, and it's because of one small thing. My classmate Harman and I both want to improve in physics, so we started a video call every evening at 7:30. We don't even talk much. We just keep our cameras on and do our own problems.

What I've noticed is this: when I'm alone, I say "five more minutes" till nine. But if I know Harman is sitting there waiting at 7:30, I'd feel embarrassed to join late. So I'm at my desk by 7:30, even on days I'm feeling lazy. Last week I had a cold and still sat down at 7:30.

Physics marks up from 52 to 68.

Your brother,
Baljeet

On the edge of the small town of Hazaribagh, Ujjwal and Ira were the only two from their college preparing for the state service exam. They lived at opposite ends of town, and the bus between them took an hour. So they made a deal at the bus stand one Sunday: every night at ten, each would send the other one message: hours studied and the topic. Ujjwal wrote the first one in the dim light of his room: "3 hrs, geography." Ira replied: "2.5, history. Tomorrow 3." Some nights the numbers were small. Night one, she had done two hours of four. "It's fine," said Siddharth. "You've been working hard. Take a break." Night two, one hour. "Honestly, me too. Let's watch one episode." By night six the check-ins were texts like "ugh, same" and "tomorrow?" Nobody pushed. The pile of unfinished chapters stayed exactly the same size. I'm Raghav, and I watched my little sister Urmila at the table. Mummy had put a red spinning top there, next to a glass of water. Urmila saw the top and her hand shot out. She did not look at the glass. Splash! Water ran over the table edge. Urmila stared at her wet sleeve and then at Mummy. I don't know if she was scared or surprised. Mummy said, "Let's wipe it together."

What did Urmila reach for?
Urmila reached for a red spinning top.
What might Urmila have felt after the splash?
Urmila may have felt surprised or startled, staring at her wet sleeve, though Raghav cannot be sure.
What could Mummy do next time?
Mummy could keep the glass away from the toy, so that wanting the toy does not lead to a spill.
How might Mummy have felt about the splash?
Mummy seemed calm, since Mummy offered to wipe it up together instead of scolding.

Saturday: Papa put all the cups on the high shelf and left only Ojas's toys on the low table. Ojas grabbed the duck straight away. Nothing spilled. He laughed.

Papa's glass of water.
How did Ojas feel when the water splashed?
He was startled and upset; he stared, then cried.
What small step helped by Saturday?
Papa put the cups on the high shelf, so Ojas could grab toys without knocking anything over.

In the small flat, Aparna set a glass of mango juice on the low table and turned to pick up the phone. Ojas, crawling nearby, spotted his bright green rattle next to the glass. His arm shot out. The glass tipped. Juice ran across the table and dripped onto the rug. Ojas froze, then patted the sticky puddle and giggled. Aparna scooped him up. "Oh, Ojas! You wanted your rattle, na?" She moved the glass to the counter.

What did Aparna set on the low table?
A glass of mango juice.

He wanted his bright green rattle; he was eager and didn't think about the glass, then seemed amused by the puddle.

Manoj looked at the photo of his cousin Rishi with a neat fringe. He wanted one too. While Mummy was in the kitchen, he found the small scissors in the drawer and snipped at his hair. Snip. It went crooked, high on one side. In the mirror his mouth began to tremble. "Mummy..." Mummy Parveen came in, took the scissors gently and put them on the high shelf. "Oh, Manoj." She hugged him. "Next time ask me first." Manoj sniffed. "I wanted to look like Rishi."

Manoj wanted a fringe like his cousin Rishi's.
How did Manoj feel when he saw the crooked fringe?
Manoj felt upset and sorry, shown by his trembling mouth.

Cousin Dev's.
What was Lalit feeling when he looked in the pot lid?

Lalit acted on his first idea without asking; next time he can ask Mumma before trying something like that.

His face fell and he looked at his desk. At break I sat with him and offered a small trick: count silently to three, then read the question again. messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday

Today in maths Miss Elizabeth asked, "What is half of 18?" and I shouted "Six!" before she even finished. Everyone laughed. It was nine. I knew it was nine. My face went hot. Afterwards Miss Elizabeth said to me, "Akash, you're quick, but try this: count one, two, three in your head, and read the question again." In English I tried it. She asked how many syllables "butterfly" has. I wanted to shout "two!" I counted one, two, three, said it in my head, but-ter-fly, and said "Three." She smiled. "Good thinking, young man." I'm going to do it tomorrow too. It feels slow but it's better than everyone laughing.

What did Akash shout when asked half of 18?
"Six!"
How did Akash feel when everyone laughed?
Akash felt embarrassed and hot in the face, especially because the right answer was known.
What else could help Akash when he feels the urge to shout?
Put a hand up first and take a breath while counting, so there's time to check the question.
How might Miss Elizabeth see the change in English?
Miss Elizabeth seems pleased and proud, smiling when the pause leads to the right answer.

messages.content:
Read this:

In the village school near Sangli, Farhan was known for his hand shooting up first. On Monday the teacher asked, "Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of stones?" "Stones!" Farhan shouted. The class burst out laughing. His friend Samir whispered, "Both are a kilo, yaar." Farhan's ears burned. That evening, walking home past the sugarcane fields, he said, "I'm going to count to three before I answer. Every time." Samir grinned. "Bet you can't." On Tuesday the teacher asked how many legs a spider has. Farhan's hand went up, but his lips moved: one, two, three. He read the question on the board again. "Eight," he said. Samir gave him a thumbs up under the desk.

What question did Farhan get wrong on Monday?
Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of stones.
How did Farhan feel when the class laughed?
He felt embarrassed; his ears burned.
What could the teacher do to help children like Farhan?
Give a few seconds of thinking time before calling on anyone, so pausing becomes normal for the whole class.
How does Samir see Farhan's new habit?
Samir teases him at first but is pleased and supportive when it works, giving a thumbs up.

Read this:

I'm Yogesh, and I still feel a little sick thinking about last Diwali. Relatives had given me festival money, and I had promised myself to keep some for school books and notebooks in June. Then an advertisement popped up: a tiny speaker with coloured lights, today only. My heart raced. I did not ask anyone, not even Lalit, who was with me at the shop. I bought it in ten minutes. It sounded fine for a week. When June came, the book fee and the notebooks were due and my pocket was empty. I had to ask Papa, who was tired after work and did not say much. That silence was worse than a scolding.

What did Yogesh buy?
Yogesh bought a tiny speaker with coloured lights.
How did Yogesh feel when June came and the pocket was empty?
Yogesh felt ashamed and regretful, and Papa's silence made it worse.
What could Yogesh do next time an advertisement tempts Yogesh?
Yogesh could wait a day and check the school needs first, or ask a trusted person before buying.

Papa may have felt tired, disappointed or worried, and chose silence over words.

Class teacher's note: Dhruv, Class 9, after the Diwali break

Dhruv came to me today, very quiet, to ask if he could pay the book fee later. When I asked gently, he explained. At Diwali he received gift money from relatives. On the same day he saw an advertisement for wireless earphones and bought them within the hour. He told me, "I didn't even think. It looked so cool." Now the book fee and three notebooks are due, and he does not want to ask his mother, Nirmala, because she had told him to keep some aside. He looked ashamed. I did not lecture him. I told him mistakes like this are common and that he should speak to his mother today; I will also mention the fee date to her myself.

What did Dhruv buy with his Diwali money?
Wireless earphones he saw in an advertisement.

He felt ashamed and worried, very quiet, afraid to face his mother after ignoring her advice.

Talk honestly with his mother today, as the teacher suggested, and next time wait a day before buying something he sees in an advertisement.

messages.content:
Read this:

In my first year of college, my allowance vanished by the third week of every month. I'm Farida, and I used to buy things the second I saw them: a phone case, a lamp, shoes I wore once. My roommate Lakshmi had a strange habit. Anything costing more than a few hundred rupees, she put in her cart and waited two days. "If I still want it on day three, I buy it." I laughed at first. Then, after a month where I couldn't afford my bus pass, I tried it. The first week, I put five things in my cart. By day three, I wanted exactly one: a proper water bottle, because mine leaked. The other four I'd forgotten about. That's still how it goes, mostly.

How many things did Farida put in the cart the first week?
Five things.
How did Farida feel after the month without a bus pass?
Farida felt worried and fed up, enough to try the waiting habit that had seemed silly before.

Ask whether it replaces something broken or needed, like the leaky bottle, and talk it over with Lakshmi if unsure.
How might Lakshmi see Farida copying her habit?
Lakshmi might feel amused, since Farida laughed at first, and quietly pleased it helped.

Hostel mentor's note: Payal, second year, October

Payal came to see me in August because she had run out of money twice in one term and felt embarrassed asking her parents again. We talked, and she decided on her own rule: anything above a set amount would sit in a list on her phone for two days before she bought it. Her friend Sonali agreed to ask her about the list each weekend. Today she showed me the list. Of fourteen items since August, she bought three: a textbook, a winter jacket and a charger. The other eleven she had deleted, saying, "By day two I didn't even remember why I wanted them." She looked relieved. I suggested she keep going and talk to her parents if a real need comes up.

How many items did Payal buy out of fourteen?
She bought three: a textbook, a winter jacket and a charger.
What was Payal feeling when she first came to the mentor in August?
She felt embarrassed and worried after running out of money twice and needing to ask her parents again.
How could Sonali keep supporting Payal?
Keep asking about the list each weekend, calmly and without judging, so Payal stays honest with herself.
How might Payal's parents be affected by her new habit?
They would likely feel relieved to get fewer urgent requests and may trust her more with her own choices.

messages.content:
Read this:

At the small rural bank branch in Satara, the morning rush had just begun when a customer's water bottle burst near the entrance. A pool spread across the tiles right where an elderly man with a walking stick was heading. Nilesh, the clerk at the first counter, didn't stop to call the cleaner or fill in the maintenance book. "Slippery floor, old man coming, ten seconds to fix," he thought, and grabbed the mop from the corner. He wiped the water in three strokes and stood the yellow sign beside it. The man stepped past safely. Gargi, at the next counter, raised her eyebrows. "You usually plan everything." Nilesh shrugged. "Not everything needs a plan. That just needed a mop."

What did Nilesh use to clean the water?
The mop from the corner, plus the yellow sign beside it.
What was Nilesh thinking when he grabbed the mop?
He felt a quick jolt of concern for the elderly man and judged it a ten-second job where speed mattered more than planning.
When would quick action like this be the wrong choice?
When a problem is big or unclear, like a leak from the ceiling, it's better to stop, call the right person and plan.
How does Gargi see Nilesh's quick move?
Gargi seems surprised and a bit amused, because he usually plans everything.

In the open-plan office in Vancouver, someone had knocked a tray of iced coffee over just outside the meeting room. Chen was on the way to a client call, laptop under one arm. He saw the brown puddle, the glass door, and the clients walking up the corridor in two minutes. "No time to find facilities or email anyone. It's just coffee on tiles." He put the laptop on a chair, grabbed a roll of paper towels from the kitchen and wiped the floor clean. Alejandro, passing with his own coffee, stopped. "Want me to log it?" "No need. It's done." The clients arrived to a dry floor. Chen picked up his laptop and walked in, slightly out of breath.

His laptop, under one arm.

He noticed the clients arriving in two minutes and walked in slightly out of breath, so he was hurried but calm about it.

Stop people walking there, then get facilities with proper tools, since that is riskier than a quick wipe.

Alejandro probably sees it as sensible, since logging a small spill would take longer than wiping it.

Tejas pulled, then pulled harder, then put a foot on the wall and pulled with both hands.

The school bus honked twice at the end of the lane. Kiran's school tie was in the bottom drawer of the old wooden almirah, and the drawer was stuck. He pushed it in and yanked it out. It moved a finger's width. He yanked harder. Nothing. He threw his whole weight back. The almirah rocked and a steel tumbler fell off the top. His sister Sarika poked her head in. "Lift it a bit, it's catching on something." "It just needs more force," Kiran grunted, and pulled again, red in the face. The bus honked a third time. Sarika slid her hand into the gap, lifted the drawer's front, and it rolled out smoothly. A crumpled tie had been caught in the runner.

A crumpled tie.

He felt frustrated and stubborn, sure that more force would work, and panicky about the bus.

Stop pulling and look into the gap, or lift the front slightly, since something may be caught.
How does Sarika see Kiran's struggle?
Sarika sees the problem quickly, perhaps a little impatient or amused that he wouldn't listen.

He braced his foot against the desk leg and pulled so hard his fingers hurt. The drawer stayed shut. Hiroshi kicked the desk and pulled again, the same way, even harder. The doorbell rang. A bent card.

He was angry and frustrated, but instead of trying something new he just pulled harder.

Ashwin sat with the notes for five hours and read every page twice.

41 in chemistry and 38 in physics.

Page after page, the same pages, three times each. Last term he did that for maths, science, everything. His marks came back: mostly in the forties. He sat on the bed staring at the report card. I said, "Why don't you try the practice questions? Close the book and see what you remember." He shook his head. "Reading is how I study." His notebooks and a highlighter.

Try closing the book and answering practice questions for one chapter, to see if recalling works better than rereading.

Then I noticed something. When I read, everything felt easy. When I tried an actual question, I couldn't even start. So reading wasn't teaching me to remember.
That night I read for twenty minutes, closed the book and wrote what I could recall. The gaps were obvious. I did practice questions for the gaps.
Next test I got 34. Mrs Kulkarni asked what had changed, and I said, I stopped rereading and started recalling. She looked surprised, and pleased.

Dev got 18 out of 50.

Mrs Kulkarni looked surprised and pleased when she asked what had changed and heard about the switch to recalling.

I'm Noor, and I sit next to Chetan in Class 10. After the half-yearly exams he got 44 in biology, and I saw his face drop. He usually says nothing, but this time he turned to me and asked, "What do you do differently?" I told him I cover my notes and try to write the answers, then check. He looked doubtful. Two weeks later I noticed he'd stopped reading from the book at lunch. Instead he had flashcards, and he'd mutter, flip one, frown, flip back. Sometimes he'd ask me to quiz him. In the unit test he got 67. He didn't say much, just showed me the paper and grinned.

What mark did Chetan get in biology at the half-yearly?
He got 44 in biology.

He probably felt disappointed and a bit desperate, ready to swallow some pride and look for another way.

Mix in past exam questions and explain answers aloud to a friend, which is more recall practice.

Two weeks later: The next test came back: 62. Shankar looked at it, then at the stack of practice questions on his desk. Rereading had felt like work. Recalling was actually working.

Asking what to change and switching to answering from memory, because it showed his gaps instead of just feeling familiar.

So, you asked about the worst decision I made as event head. It was the date. I'm Ritika, and I'd announced the fest for the fourteenth on the notice board and in the group chat, with a poster and everything.
Five days before, the hall cancelled. My team said, move it a week. I said no. I'd told the whole college. They showed me the calendar, the exam schedule, everything, and I just kept saying, the fourteenth is the fourteenth.
So we ran it in the open courtyard, at noon, with a borrowed speaker. The heat sent half the audience away, and our guest was late. Danish, our treasurer, didn't speak to me for days.
Honestly? I wasn't protecting the fest. I was protecting my announcement.

I'm Kishore, the cultural secretary's assistant, so I saw all of it. Payal had announced the inter-college music night for 14 March on every group and on the college page. Then, ten days before, the auditorium cancelled; the hall was needed for exams. We had options. The open-air theatre was free on the 21st, and the principal was happy to help. At the meeting, Payal cut us off. "We said the 14th. Everyone knows the 14th. We're not changing." She booked a small seminar hall that held eighty. Two hundred people came. Half stood in the corridor, the sound was terrible, and two bands left. Payal smiled for photos, but afterwards I saw her sitting alone on the steps.

Eighty, though two hundred people came.

She probably felt ashamed and upset, knowing the evening went badly because she refused to move the date.

Moving to the open-air theatre on the 21st and announcing the change honestly, because the facts had changed and people accept a clear reason.

The bands faced a cramped hall and terrible sound; two were frustrated enough to leave.

Tuesday, lab, 9 pm

Attempt eleven failed. The cells didn't glow at all this time. Rashmi packed up at seven and said, "Maybe the effect just isn't real, Dolma." I sat with the notebook for a long time after she left. But three separate papers have seen it. And in attempt six we saw a faint signal, twice. So it's probably real and I'm doing something wrong. Not the same wrong thing, I hope. Let me list what I've changed: temperature (attempt 4), timing (7), the dye batch (9). What I haven't touched: how long the cells rest before treatment. Tomorrow: rest them for two hours instead of thirty minutes. One change only. If eleven failures taught me anything, it's not to change five things at once.

Eleven; attempt eleven failed.

Dolma feels discouraged but still hopeful, because three papers and the faint signal in attempt six suggest the effect is real.

Each attempt changes one detail, like the resting time, instead of repeating the same experiment.

Madhav, you're stuck choosing between electives? Let me tell you about your Madhuri Bua at fifteen. I had to pick between biology and computer science for Class 11. I asked my teachers. Then my cousins. Then the neighbours' son, the one who became a doctor. I read every newspaper article I could find about jobs. Saturday: At his friend Suraj's house, Amandeep found an old board game with no rule sheet: wooden pegs, a board of holes and coloured tiles. Suraj shrugged. "Nobody knows how it works."

Sunday: Amandeep came back. "Let's just try moves and see what happens. If it's wrong, who cares? It's only a game." He moved a peg two holes. Nothing. He jumped it over a tile. Suraj gasped. "Maybe that captures it!"

The next Saturday: The boys had invented a full set of rules through trying. Jumping captured tiles, and corners were safe. They'd played eleven rounds. "I think we made it better than the real one," Amandeep said, grinning.

How many rounds had the boys played by the next Saturday?
Eleven rounds.
Why was Amandeep happy to just try moves?
He felt relaxed and curious, because mistakes cost nothing and playing was the fun part.
When would trial and error not be the best approach?
When mistakes are costly or unsafe, like with electricity or money, asking an adult or reading instructions is better.
How does Suraj see the game by the end?
Suraj seems excited and proud, having helped invent rules for a game nobody understood.
