Since you'll be running next year's alumni day, here's how we did this one, step by step.
First, one long Friday afternoon, all six of us just threw out ideas: a quiz, a cricket match, a slide show of old photos, lunch in the hostel mess. We wrote down thirty-one without arguing about any.
Second, we made a grid. Each idea got marks for how many alumni it would pull in, how much work it needed, and whether rain could ruin it. The photo show and the mess lunch won; cricket lost on rain.
Third, we turned the winners into a checklist with names and dates: book the mess by the 5th, collect photos by the 12th, test the projector the day before.
It wasn't perfect. The projector still failed for ten minutes. But nothing big was forgotten.
Good luck with it,
Tenzin

What made cricket lose on the grid?
Cricket lost on rain.
How does Tenzin seem to feel about how the day went?
Tenzin sounds satisfied but honest: pleased that nothing big was forgotten, while admitting the projector still failed.
What would you add to the checklist next time, and why?
A backup for the projector, such as printed photos or a spare laptop, since the checklist tested it but had no plan if it failed anyway.
What is it like for Varun to receive this email?
Varun gets a clear map for next year, which could make running the alumni day feel less daunting and shows which method to use at which step 😊

metadata.subtype: Approach: combines methods in one project: brainstorm, matrix, then a checklist [Action]

Read this:

Afreen, head of the customer support department, had to bring in a new shift system. She could have simply announced it, but she called the team to the meeting room.
"This changes everyone's week," she said. "If you don't accept it, it won't work, so tell me what you think."
Tarun raised a point about late finishes and bus timings. Others asked about weekends. The meeting ran forty minutes over.
The next Monday she came back with a changed rota: shorter late shifts and alternate weekends. It took two weeks longer than announcing it would have, but the team accepted it and hardly anyone asked to swap.

How long did the meeting run over?
The meeting ran forty minutes over.
What was Afreen feeling when she asked the team for their views?
Afreen was probably concerned that the team would reject the change, since she said it won't work if they don't accept it.
What could Afreen do if some staff still dislike the new rota?
Afreen could hold a short review after a month and adjust the rota, since the team's acceptance decides whether it works.
How might Tarun feel after the changed rota?
Tarun raised the bus timings and saw shorter late shifts come back, so may feel listened to.

"So that's the draft," Parveen said, turning the whiteboard toward the nine lab staff. "Two rotating shifts instead of fixed ones. Before I send it up, I want to hear what breaks."
Jasleen crossed her arms. "Madam, honestly? Rotating every week will be very hard for anyone with small kids."
"Say more."
"School drop-offs. If I'm on early one week and late the next, I can't plan anything with my mother-in-law."
Another technician called from the back, "And the last bus goes at ten."
Parveen wrote both on the board. "Okay. What if the rotation is monthly, not weekly? And we check the bus times before fixing the late shift?"
"Monthly I could manage," Jasleen said slowly.
"This will take two more weeks than I planned," Parveen admitted. "But if you all hate it, it won't work anyway. We meet again Friday."

When does the last bus go?
The last bus goes at ten.
What was Parveen feeling when admitting the delay?
Parveen seemed a little uneasy about losing two weeks, but calm and sure it was worth it, since the staff hating the plan would make it fail.
What else could Parveen do before Friday?
Parveen could check the bus times and quietly ask staff who didn't speak up, so the next draft reflects everyone and not just the loudest voices.
How does Jasleen see being asked before the change?
Jasleen feels able to speak honestly, and by the end is open to a monthly rotation, because the real problem was heard and written on the board.

Read this:

When management asked me to bring in a new shift pattern for the front office, my first thought was to design it myself over a weekend. I know the numbers; I've done the rosters for three years. But I kept picturing the notice going up and twelve people reading it in silence, then quietly swapping duties among themselves. So I asked instead. I held two short meetings, one for the day staff and one at midnight for the night desk. Lakshmi, who has been at the hotel longer than I have, said, "Pallavi ma'am, nobody minds nights. They mind not knowing until Sunday which nights." That changed everything. The fix was publishing the roster two weeks ahead, not the pattern itself. It took a month instead of a weekend. The new roster started last week, and so far only one swap request has come in.

How far ahead is the roster now published?
The roster is published two weeks ahead.
What was Pallavi worried might happen if the pattern was designed alone?
Pallavi was worried the twelve staff would read the notice in silence and quietly swap duties among themselves, so the plan would fail without anyone saying so.
Why might the slower approach work better than a weekend plan?
Because the staff helped find the real problem, they are more likely to accept the roster, and the single swap request so far suggests it is working.
How might Lakshmi feel about being asked?
Lakshmi likely feels respected and trusted, able to point out the real issue: not knowing until Sunday which nights to work.

When the letter about the boundary of her late grandfather's flat arrived, Dolma did not try to work it out herself. She had never dealt with anything like it.
That evening she gathered every paper she could find: the old sale deed, the tax receipts, two letters from the neighbour. She sorted them by date in a folder and listed what was missing.
On Saturday she took the folder to an advocate, Uday, and said, "I don't know what this means and I don't want to guess." Uday read for twenty minutes, asked for a survey copy and explained the next steps.
Dolma left with a list of documents to find, feeling less alone with it, though nothing was settled.

What did Dolma take to the advocate?
Dolma took a folder of papers sorted by date.
What did Dolma feel about the letter, and why did she not guess?
Dolma felt unsure because she had never dealt with anything like it, and she did not want to guess.
What could Dolma do while waiting to find the missing documents?
Dolma could keep the folder in order and note each document she finds, since the advocate needs the full set to help.
How might Uday see Dolma's way of coming to the meeting?
Uday received a folder sorted by date with a list of what was missing, so probably found it easier to start work.

"Tenzin, look at this." Seema spread the letter on the table. "The neighbour next to Nana's plot says our wall is on his land now. He wants us to sign something. Amma says since I'm the granddaughter living nearest, I should handle it."
"So write back and tell him he's wrong."
"That's what I wanted to do last night. Then I saw I don't even know where the boundary is. I've never read the land papers."
"Where are they?"
"Amma has the sale deed. The survey map is at the taluka office. I called Amma this morning; she's sending photos of the deed."
"Then what?"
"Then I'm not signing and I'm not arguing. I've booked an hour with a property lawyer on Thursday. I'll take everything: deed, map, this letter, the old tax receipts."
"Feels slow."
"It is slow. But if I guess wrong here, it's Nana's land. I'd rather be slow."

When is the meeting with the property lawyer?
On Thursday; Seema has booked an hour with a property lawyer.
Why did Seema hold back from writing to the neighbour?
Seema felt unsure and anxious, having realised the boundary was unclear and the land papers were unread, and worried about getting it wrong on Nana's land.
What else could help Seema make good use of that hour?
Writing a short list of questions and a timeline of when the letter came, so the lawyer can see the facts quickly and nothing is forgotten.
How does Tenzin see Seema's plan?
Tenzin finds it slow and at first wants a quick reply telling the neighbour he is wrong, but the plan is explained as the safer path.

When the society notice came saying my balcony grille broke building rules and had to go within the month, my first instinct was to fight it on the residents' group. Suraj, my colleague, even offered to draft a strong reply; he'd "handled a landlord once". I almost let him. Then Papa said on the phone, "Sangeeta beti, don't sign or send anything in a hurry." I read the notice again and understood maybe half of it. So I went step by step. I found the purchase agreement and the builder's approved plan in Papa's steel cupboard. I asked the society office, politely, for the rule they were quoting, in writing. I photographed the grille and the builder's letter. Then I booked one session with a lawyer who handles housing matters. It turned out the grille was in the approved plan. I'm glad Suraj's reply was never sent.

Where did Sangeeta find the purchase agreement?
In Papa's steel cupboard.
How did Sangeeta feel on first reading the notice?
Sangeeta was upset and ready to fight it, then uneasy on realising only about half of the notice made sense.
Which step did the most to settle the matter, and why?
Finding the builder's approved plan and taking it to a lawyer, because it showed the grille was allowed, which arguing on the residents' group never could.
How might Suraj feel when the grille turns out to be in the approved plan?
Suraj might feel a little sheepish that the strong reply would have been wrong, and perhaps relieved it was never sent.

Thursday night in the hostel common room, three friends and one visitor had their laptops open. Varun read out a message from his professor: she wanted to talk about his essay, because parts of it sounded machine-written. His stomach dropped. Two paragraphs had been drafted by a chatbot and then tidied by him, so he decided to bring his notes and chat history to the meeting and ask what the department allowed. Jahnavi barely looked up. She was typing to her AI companion about a rotten day, and it answered warmly every time, never tired, never critical. "Easier than ringing anyone," she said, then added, "though I haven't replied to Nisha in two weeks." Yusuf pasted a chatbot's summary of a tax rule into his slides. "It sounds so sure," he said, then frowned. "I'll find the real source before I present." From the sofa, Ritu scrolled job listings for her design course and read one aloud that mentioned automation. "Will there be any work for me at all?" she asked. 😟

What did Varun's professor say about his essay?
The professor said parts of it sounded machine-written and wanted to talk about it.
How do Varun's plan for the meeting and Yusuf's plan for his slides show a similar careful approach to AI tools?

Both take responsibility for what the AI produced: Varun will bring his notes and chat history and be honest about his process, while Yusuf will look for the real source instead of accepting a confident answer.
What was Varun feeling when he read the professor's message, and how can you tell?
He felt exposed and anxious; his stomach dropped, and he quickly began planning what to bring to the meeting.
What could Jahnavi do to keep her human friendships growing alongside her companion?
She could reply to Nisha and arrange to talk or meet, enjoying the companion's comfort without letting it replace her friends. 🙂

Read this:

Anand, the team lead, closed the Monday review with a smile. "Nobody is as dependable as you, Tushar," he said, and dropped two more client accounts on Tushar's plate. Tushar nodded, though he had been finishing reports at midnight for a month. That evening he ate in silence and snapped when the tap dripped. Vikas, his partner, felt the chill but did not take it personally. "I miss you," he said softly. "Could we keep Sunday breakfast, phones away?" Tushar agreed, guiltily. A few days later his friend Ritu caught him yawning over a lunch he barely touched. "You look flattened. Go home and rest," she said. He almost laughed it off, then only said, "Yeah. Okay. A walk after work, maybe?" By the lake he admitted that most mornings felt hollow. The next week he sat in a clinic and told the doctor everything: the poor sleep, the skipped meals, the low mood, the late nights he had been hiding. The doctor listened and set up follow-up visits. Back at work, Tushar wrote down every task he held and asked Anand which ones mattered most.

What did Anand do at the end of the Monday review?
He said nobody is as dependable as Tushar and dropped two more client accounts on his plate.
How did Vikas's response to Tushar's exhaustion differ from Anand's?
Anand praised Tushar's dependability while adding more accounts, whereas Vikas said softly that he missed him and suggested keeping Sunday breakfast, caring for Tushar rather than using his effort.
How was Tushar likely feeling when he agreed to the Sunday breakfast, and what shows it?
He was probably guilty and worn down; he agreed guiltily right after snapping at home and eating in silence.
What could Tushar keep doing to stay well after the clinic visit?
He could keep small rituals like Sunday breakfast and lakeside walks, attend the follow-up visits, and keep asking Anand which tasks matter most. 🙂

Six-year-old Vaibhav sat on the doorstep holding Nani's shawl. "Who will tell me the crocodile story now?" he asked. His mother, Bidisha, said, "Nani has died, and she cannot come back. I miss her too." He asked again the next morning, and she answered again in the same plain words. On Sunday the house filled with relatives. Aunties chopped vegetables in the kitchen, uncles sat on the floor reading prayers, and some people cried while others passed around tea. His father, Tejas, carried in a big pot of rice. Vaibhav did not follow the words, but he leaned against his uncle's arm and stayed. Later he found the photo album and stopped at Dada, who had died the winter before and used to keep toffees in his pocket for him. "Dada gave me sweets," he said, smiling and wiping his eyes. Bidisha helped him draw Dada holding a giant toffee. That night, in the dark, he whispered, "Mummy, will you die too?" Bidisha lay down beside him. "Everybody dies one day, but most people live a very long time. Papa and I are here, and we will always look after you." He held her hand until he fell asleep.

What was Vaibhav holding when he sat on the doorstep?
He was holding Nani's shawl.
How did Vaibhav's feelings at night differ from what he felt looking at Dada's photo, and what helped each?

Looking at Dada's photo he felt warm and sad together, and drawing Dada with a toffee helped; at night he was frightened and asked if Mummy would die, and calm honest words that most people live a long time helped.
What might Vaibhav have been feeling when he whispered his question in the dark?
He was probably frightened; he asked in the dark and held Bidisha's hand until he fell asleep.
Which choice by Bidisha helped Vaibhav with his grief, and why?
She answered his repeated questions in the same plain words, so he could ask again and feel safe and looked after.

After Pallavi moved to a new school, lunch was the loneliest hour. At night a stranger in a music group chat was kind to her, always asking about her day. "Don't mention me to anyone," the stranger wrote one week. "Nobody would understand us." Devika noticed Pallavi hiding her phone and jumping at every buzz. "You've gone quiet," she said. "I'm not cross, just worried. Want to show me?" Pallavi did. The stranger had asked for a picture and, once she sent it, wrote that it would go to her whole class unless she sent more. Devika did not scold. "This isn't your fault," she said. "Don't reply, don't pay, don't send anything. Let's save every message." They took screenshots together, and before the bell Devika walked her to the counsellor. The counsellor sat with Pallavi, told her the shame belonged to the person making threats, and called her parents and the cybercrime helpline that same afternoon. Kunal, at the next table, had overheard. He had been chatting with a gaming friend for months and badly wanted to meet. That evening he told his mother, who said they could meet at a busy cafe with her sitting nearby. When the friend replied, "Come alone and keep it secret," Kunal stopped replying.

Where did Pallavi meet the stranger who was kind to her?
She met the stranger in a music group chat.
How did Kunal's handling of his online friend differ from what happened to Pallavi with her stranger?

Kunal told his mother, planned a busy cafe with her nearby, and stopped replying when asked for secrecy; Pallavi hid her phone and was pressured to send a picture, and only became safer when Devika helped her save the messages and see the counsellor.
What might Pallavi have felt in the days before she showed Devika, and how can you tell?
She was probably afraid and anxious, since she hid her phone and jumped at every buzz.
What small steps did Devika take that made it safer for Pallavi to get help?
She listened without scolding, said it was not Pallavi's fault, told her not to reply or pay, saved the messages, and walked her to the counsellor.

Read this:

Vikas had one new rule: both boys home before sunset, since a scooter had skidded near the market. Francis, fourteen, went straight to work. His eyes filled, his voice wobbled, and he called his father the best in the street. It worked once, and afterwards the sweetness sat in his mouth like something borrowed. Anand, sixteen, went the loud way. "You treat us like babies!" he shouted, and his bedroom door rattled. The next evening he tried again, quietly. "The team practises at the ground then, and I need to be there. I know the road scares you. Could I message when I leave and when I arrive?" Vikas said he would think. Francis, meanwhile, refused to speak at dinner for three days and left his maths book shut, as though that would punish anyone. On the fourth night Anand sat beside his father. "What exactly are you afraid will happen?" Vikas rubbed his forehead. "A truck. Bad company. People talking if you are out late." "Then let's fix those," Anand said. "Try me for two weeks." Vikas looked at the boys, and slowly nodded.

What happened near the market that led to Vikas's new rule?
A scooter had skidded near the market.
How did Francis's first move differ from Anand's second try, and which fits better with earning trust?

Francis's eyes filled and he called his father the best in the street, and it worked once, but the sweetness felt borrowed; Anand said he needed to be at the ground, knew the road scares his father, and offered to message when he leaves and arrives, so the quiet honest try fits better with trust.
How was Francis feeling during the three silent days at dinner?
He was resentful and angry, which he showed by refusing to speak and leaving his maths book shut.
What could Francis try instead of tears or silence?
He could say calmly what the rule costs him and ask for a trial, as Anand did, so his father can see he takes the fear seriously.

Read this:

Anirban waved his phone at Ira. "Come to the rally on Saturday, or you're not really with us," he said, and urged her to repost a furious slogan. Ira had not read the petition behind it. She read it that night, agreed with half, and shared only the part she could stand behind. At dinner she asked her mother, Madhuri, about Saturday. "No," Madhuri said at once. "Crowds turn, and I would be sick with worry." Ira felt her ears burn but said, "I hear you. Could I write letters to the council and sell bookmarks to pay for banners instead?" Madhuri thought, then nodded. In the corridor a classmate laughed. "Posters won't save a lake, Ira. Pointless." Ira took a breath and pulled out her printed figures. "Last time, forty families wrote in and the council changed the drain plan. It's slow, but it moves." That night her stomach twisted at the thought of a teacher calling the students troublemakers, or police turning up. She told Madhuri, and they read together what the rules for peaceful gatherings allowed. Being scared, Madhuri said, did not make anyone a coward.

What did Ira offer her mother instead of going to the rally?
She offered to write letters to the council and sell bookmarks to pay for banners.
How did Madhuri treat Ira's wish to help differently from how Anirban pushed her?

Anirban told Ira she was not really with them unless she came and reposted a furious slogan, while Madhuri said no to the rally but agreed to letters and bookmarks, and later read the rules with Ira and said being scared did not make anyone a coward.
What was Ira feeling that night when she thought about teachers and police?
She felt afraid of the consequences; her stomach twisted, and she chose to tell Madhuri.
What could Ira do next to keep helping the cause?
She could keep writing letters and selling bookmarks, and keep gathering facts for anyone who calls it pointless. 🙂

Read this:

Nine-year-old Wasim sat on the back step with an empty water bowl in his lap. Biscuit, his dog, had died in the night, and the crying would not stop. His father, Jeevan, sat down beside him and wrapped an arm around his shoulders. "It's okay to cry," Jeevan said. "I'm sad too." Wasim felt a little less alone. Later, in a low voice, he told his aunt Keerthana, "Biscuit didn't finish his dinner on Sunday and I didn't tell anyone. If I'd noticed, maybe he'd still be here." Keerthana put down the vegetables. "Wasim, lots of children think they should have saved a pet. But you walked him, washed him and gave him your biscuits every single day. That's how much you loved him." That evening Wasim found a shoebox and filled it with the red collar, a photo and the tennis ball. He wrote BISCUIT on the lid, and Jeevan helped him choose a shelf where it could stay.

What did Wasim put in the shoebox?
He put in the red collar, a photo and the tennis ball.
How did Jeevan's response to Wasim's crying differ from Keerthana's response to his guilty thought?

Jeevan sat beside him and said it was okay to cry, which made Wasim feel less alone, while Keerthana answered his guilt by reminding him how he walked, washed and gave his biscuits to Biscuit every day.
What was Wasim feeling when he told Keerthana about the dinner, and how can you tell?
He felt guilty; he spoke in a low voice and wondered if noticing sooner would have kept Biscuit here.
What could Wasim and Jeevan do with the shoebox in the weeks ahead?
They could look at it together and share stories about Biscuit whenever Wasim feels sad.

Read this:

The bank-exam form sat on the dining table like a bill. Himani knew her father, Jatin, had worn the same watch for eleven years so her fees could be paid, and the thought sat heavy on her chest. "Your cousin Francis just got his first salary," her mother said, buttering toast. "Forty thousand." Himani set her cup down. "Ma, when you say that, I hear that I'm not enough. It hurts." Her mother blinked and went quiet. Himani did not spend the evening resenting Francis; she texted him congratulations. Later she sat with her father. "Papa, why do you want the bank job for me? I'd like to hear it before I decide. I'm thinking of design, and we may not agree." Jatin talked about the year his shop closed and the fear that followed. She listened, then said, "I'll prepare for the exam and I'll apply to the studio. Either way, the decision is mine." Walking home, she realised the man who always seemed certain had been frightened all along, and had sometimes snapped at her mother for no reason. She felt a small sadness for the father in her head, and a new warmth for the one who lived with them.

Whose first salary did Himani's mother mention?
She mentioned her cousin Francis's first salary.
How did Himani's reaction to the comparison with Francis differ from how she spoke with her father about the bank job?
With her mother she said the comparison hurt and then congratulated Francis instead of resenting him; with her father she asked for his reasons, disagreed politely, and said the decision was hers.
What was Himani feeling as she thought about her father's watch?
She felt grateful and burdened at once, because the thought sat heavy on her chest.
What could Himani do to honour her parents' effort while keeping her choice?
She could prepare for the exam and apply to the studio, keep listening to her father's reasons, and make the final decision herself.

Read this:

When the coach read out the new debate captain, it was Gopika's name. Zeenat's stomach clenched. She had wanted that badge for two years. That night she admitted the envy to herself, then watched a recording of Gopika's last round and wrote down how she opened with a story and paused before every rebuttal. At the next practice Zeenat asked her for tips, and they argued the same motion from opposite sides, grinning whenever a point landed. Nazia stood by the door. "You only got it because the coach likes you," she told Gopika. Gopika went hot, because a small voice in her had wondered the same. She did not snap back. After practice she asked the coach for honest feedback on her speeches and left with three things to work on. Nazia could not bear even hearing Gopika's name, and her jaw tightened whenever it came up in the team chat. She realised she had thought about nothing else all week, and her own speech on water saving was still half-written. She closed the chat and opened her notebook. 🙂

What did Zeenat write down after watching Gopika's recording?
She wrote down that Gopika opened with a story and paused before every rebuttal.
How did Zeenat's response to Gopika winning differ from Nazia's?
Zeenat admitted her envy, studied Gopika's round and became friendly, while Nazia could not bear Gopika's name and sneered at her; only later did she turn back to her own speech.
What was Gopika feeling when Nazia said the coach liked her, and why did it sting?
She felt hot with hurt, because a small voice in her had wondered the same thing.
What could Nazia do to stop her feelings from draining her energy?
She could keep her attention on her own speech and goals, as she did when she opened her notebook, rather than on Gopika.

Read this:

In the office pantry, a senior colleague mimicked Jatin's accent and joked that people from his region never finish anything on time. Others chuckled. Shreya laughed weakly too, then said nothing. Jatin's face went hot. He set down his cup and left. All afternoon Shreya's chest felt tight. That evening she messaged him: "I should have said something. Are you okay?" Jatin wrote back that a landlord had turned him away that same week; the man had looked at his surname and said the flat was taken. Jatin felt angry and small, though he knew it said more about the landlord than about him. Shreya helped him list other flats, and they wrote down the dates of both incidents. The next morning, when the same colleague made another joke, Shreya said evenly, "That's not funny." Jatin later took his notes to a senior in HR. Devika, who had watched all this, had caught herself that week assuming the new hire from the north would be rude. She noticed the thought without punishing herself, sat beside him at lunch, and found him funnier and kinder than her guess.

What did Shreya message Jatin that evening?
She wrote that she should have said something and asked if he was okay.
How did Shreya's second reaction to the colleague's jokes differ from her first, and what had changed?
The first time she laughed weakly and said nothing; the next morning she said evenly, "That's not funny," after feeling tight-chested all afternoon and checking on Jatin.
How did Jatin feel when the landlord said the flat was taken, and what did he understand about it?
He felt angry and small, though he knew the refusal said more about the landlord than about him.
What could Devika keep doing to test her own assumptions about people?
She could keep sitting with people, as she did at lunch, and compare her guesses with what they are actually like.

Read this:

Before the bell, Karthik leaned over Baljeet's desk. "Lend me your maths homework. Real friends let each other copy, you know." Baljeet's stomach flipped; he did want to help. "I am your friend," he said. "That's why I'll show you how to do the first sum, and then you try the rest." Karthik grumbled, but at recess they sat together and got three sums done. In art class Shreya groaned, having forgotten her colours. Baljeet slid his box across the desk without a second thought. By afternoon the box had not come back, so he asked, "Could I have my colours, please? I need the blue." She apologised and returned them at once. At lunch Ritesh sat beside him, chatty and full of jokes, and shared half a mango. Ten minutes later he asked to borrow Baljeet's new pen, then his eraser. Baljeet realised Ritesh had not spoken to him all week. "Sorry, I need them today," he said, and left it at that.

What did Baljeet lend Shreya in art class?
He lent her his box of colours.
How did Baljeet's answer to Karthik differ from his reaction when Shreya needed colours, and why?

He would not hand over his homework and offered to show Karthik the first sum so he could learn, but he freely lent Shreya his colours, a small loan, and politely asked for them back when they were late.
What was Baljeet likely feeling when Ritesh asked for the pen and then the eraser?
He probably felt used, because Ritesh had not spoken to him all week and was friendly only when he wanted something.
What could Baljeet say next time a friend uses guilt to ask for answers?
He could say he is their friend and will teach them, then offer to sit together and work it out. 🙂

Read this:

The class group chat lit up at nine. Chaitanya had written, "Kiran's talk was so dull I nearly slept." Kiran's ears burned, and his thumbs hovered over a reply that would humiliate Chaitanya in front of forty people. He put the phone down, drank some water, then opened a private chat. "That comment stung. Can we talk?" A minute later came: "Sorry. It was a stupid joke." The next day a rumour appeared: Vinita had copied her science project. Her first instinct was to delete the app and vanish. Instead she told her mother and the class teacher, then wrote one message in the group with her draft and its dates attached, and let it stand. Two friends sat with her at lunch. That evening someone shared a voice note of a shy boy, Ravi, stumbling over a poem, and the chat filled with laughing faces. Chaitanya typed a mocking line too, because he did not want to be the next target. The moment he sent it, his stomach dropped. He deleted it, but people had already seen it, so he messaged Ravi: "That was unkind of me. I liked your poem." 🙂

How many people were in the class group chat?
Forty people were there.
How did Kiran's way of handling Chaitanya's harsh comment differ from Chaitanya's behaviour toward Ravi's voice note?
Kiran put the phone down and took his hurt to a private chat, while Chaitanya joined the public mocking for fear of being next and only afterwards sent Ravi a private apology.

Before it could burst, she knocked on his door on Saturday. "Hi, I've been getting annoyed and I'd rather say so than stew. Could the bike go by the gate, and could drilling wait until ten?"

Kishore had had a bad week. He felt accused in front of the open stairwell and his voice went up. "You live in a flat, what do you expect? Everyone parks wherever!" Reena felt her own temper rise and her fingers tighten on the railing. She breathed and said, "I hear you. This isn't a good moment. Can we talk tomorrow, just the two of us?" She stepped away from the neighbours peering out of their doors.

At night Kishore realised he'd shouted about something that was not really about the bike. Next morning he came upstairs with a scrap of paper. "I'll park by the gate and stop drilling before ten. Sorry about yesterday." Reena nodded. She told herself that if the shouting had continued she would have gone to Sharmila on the society committee, but it did not come to that.

What did Reena ask Kishore to do about his bike?
She asked him to park the bike by the gate.
How did Reena's calm request and Kishore's raised voice look from each side?

Reena spoke early, before her irritation burst, and stayed calm when he shouted, offering to talk privately later. Kishore felt accused in front of neighbours and shouted, then realised it was about more than the bike and came with a fix.
What was Reena feeling when Kishore raised his voice on the stairwell?
She felt angry, her temper rising and her fingers tightening on the railing, but she chose to breathe.
What could Reena do if Kishore starts shouting again next month?
She could stay calm, listen, offer to talk later away from an audience, and ask Sharmila on the society committee to help if it keeps escalating.

When Charu started explaining the savings sheet she had made, Yogesh rolled his eyes. "Here we go, the accountant." He mimicked the way she hummed while she chopped onions, and felt superior and very tired. It was easier than saying that he had been feeling unseen since the job changed.

Charu felt herself shrink. She stopped in the middle of a sentence, and for a moment she thought about answering in kind, with a sneer of her own. She swallowed it. Speaking felt risky, as if anything she said would be turned into a joke. She told her friend Ishita about it at lunch, and Ishita said, "That's a pattern, not one bad evening."

That night Charu said, quietly, "When you roll your eyes and copy me, I feel small. I would like us to talk with respect. If this keeps happening, I would like to see a counsellor together."

Yogesh went quiet. Then, after a while, he said, "I've been feeling like nobody notices what I do since the transfer, and I took it out on you. I'm sorry." He turned off the television. "Tell me about the sheet."

Where did Charu tell Ishita about it?
She told Ishita at lunch.
How did Yogesh's eye-rolling look from his side and from Charu's side?

Yogesh felt superior and tired but was really hiding that he felt unseen, while Charu felt small and unsafe to speak. She named the pattern and asked for respect, and he then named the hurt beneath it.
What was Charu feeling when she stopped in the middle of her sentence?
She felt small and unsafe to speak, afraid her words would be turned into a joke.
What could Charu do if Yogesh's sneering returns after this talk?
She could calmly point to the pattern again, ask for respect without sneering back, and suggest they see a counsellor together.

How did Francis's small first disclosure and Yogesh's quiet reactions connect to the bigger conversation on the balcony?

What was Yogesh feeling when Francis said he had dropped out?
He felt honoured and unsure what to say, so he set aside his urge to offer solutions.

Omkar had built a tall block fort and he wanted to be the boss of it. When Minakshi came over with a flag, he put his hand up. "No girls!" A boy beside him copied him, "No girls," and then it sounded like a rule. Omkar felt big and important, and didn't think about how it landed.

Minakshi stopped. A heavy stone dropped into her tummy and her eyes prickled. She walked away and stood near the shelf, blinking hard. She thought about crying, then she went to Rukmini, the teacher, and said, "They said I can't play."

Rukmini took her hand and went over to the fort. She crouched to Omkar's level. "Omkar, if someone said 'no you' to you, how would that feel?" Omkar was quiet. "Bad," he said. "Like a stone." The teacher waited. Then he looked at Minakshi and said, in a small voice, "Come and play." Minakshi held up the flag. "Where does it go?" The other boy shuffled aside and made a gap in the wall, and the flag went on top.

What did Minakshi bring to the block fort?
She brought a flag.
How did the words no girls feel to Omkar and to Minakshi, and what did Rukmini change?
Omkar felt big and important and did not think about the hurt, while Minakshi felt a stone in her tummy. Rukmini helped Omkar remember how it feels to be told no, and he said come and play.
What was Minakshi feeling as she stood near the shelf blinking hard?
She felt hurt and sad, like a stone in her tummy, and close to crying.
How could the teacher help if the boys try to make no girls a group rule again?

How did the grabbing feel to Chaitanya and to Irfan, and what did Samir do for each?

What was Irfan feeling when he closed his tightened fist again?
He felt scared and small, and he wanted to hit back but chose not to.
What could Chaitanya try next time someone takes his toy?

She also listed what the evening would cost, and asked classmates for a small fixed amount each. When the caterer's quote was too high, she priced home-made snacks and found they would cover the difference. A shared sheet tracked every rupee spent.

Uday and Abhinav were in charge of sound and seating. "There's still time," Abhinav said, week after week. On the last afternoon they found the speakers needed a cable nobody had, and thirty chairs were still locked in another room. Parents stood at the doors while the boys ran up and down corridors, and the evening began twenty minutes late.

Then the chief guest's car got stuck in traffic. Anjali leaned to the compere: "Bring the dance forward, swap the order." The audience clapped through the folk dance, and nobody noticed a gap. Afterwards the team wrote in the sheet: next time, leave a buffer between items, and check the sound a week earlier.

How late did the evening begin?
The evening began twenty minutes late.
How did Anjali's early planning differ from what Uday and Abhinav did, and what did each lead to?
Anjali gave every step a date and tracked costs, while Uday and Abhinav waited until the last afternoon for sound and seating, so a cable and chairs were missing and the evening began late.
What were Uday and Abhinav probably feeling when they found the missing cable and chairs?
Panic and embarrassment, since parents were waiting at the doors.
What could the team do next year?
They could check the sound and seating a week earlier and leave a buffer between items.

For months Vidya said nothing when her mother-in-law Yamini arrived unannounced, sometimes twice in a week. She smiled, put the kettle on, and cleared her afternoon. Then one evening Yamini said, mildly, "You should use less oil," and Vidya snapped, "Nothing I do is right in this house!" The kitchen went silent. Yamini left early, and Vidya's husband Kunal stared at his plate.

That night Vidya thought about it. Yamini had tried to cook at every visit, even when Vidya had already cooked. Perhaps it was Yamini's way of feeling needed, and Vidya wondered about asking for one special dish each time.

With Kunal, she first settled what they both wanted: a call before visits, and holidays split fairly. Only then did Kunal talk to his parents, saying "we" throughout, and they heard one voice, not two against them.

Diwali was still tense. Afterwards the couple wrote down what helped: Yamini's special dish, the phone calls; and what did not: two big meals in two days. Next year they would host one meal and travel for the other, and stay kinder to everybody.

What did Yamini say before Vidya snapped?
Yamini said, "You should use less oil."
How did Vidya's silence about the visits differ in effect from the couple's joint plan?
Her silence let resentment build until a mild comment set off an outburst, while agreeing a shared position first let Kunal speak for both, so his parents heard one voice.
What was Vidya feeling when she snapped?
Built-up resentment and hurt, released by a small comment after months of saying nothing.
What could Vidya and Kunal do to include Yamini?
They could ask Yamini to make one special dish each visit and agree on a call before visits.

What interrupted Vinita's chanting on the walk home?

How did Jagdish's way of remembering differ from Seema's, and what happened to each?

Jagdish asked his father to quiz him that night and counted the items off on his fingers, while Seema trusted her memory, wrote nothing, and could recall only three of four items and could not reach her classmate.
What was Seema feeling with the crease between her eyebrows?

Madhav found it under the bus seat.

What did Keerthana drop from her list?
She dropped the club event.
How did Keerthana plan her week differently from Anand, and why did hers hold together?

Keerthana ranked tasks by deadline and marks and left empty half-hours for surprises, so the lab redo fitted in, while Anand kept saying two hours and starting late until he made every guess half as long again.
What was Anand feeling at six in the morning?
Exhausted and probably frustrated, still typing with a cold cup of tea beside him.
What could Anand do to keep the habit going?
Anand could keep making his guesses half as long again and check them against how long tasks really took.

Manoj stretched for just ten minutes and jogged slowly to the corner and back. On bad days, the stretching alone counted. Each week he added a few minutes, and by March his jog reached the park.

Jeevan, motivated on the first of January, paid for a full year at a gym and planned hard workouts every day. Then a cold and a crowded work week broke his streak. He looked at the calendar, felt like a failure, and never went back.

What was Rekha's signal to start walking?
Her signal was putting down the toothbrush.
How did Jeevan's plan differ from Manoj's, and what happened when each hit a bad week?

Jeevan planned hard daily workouts and dropped everything after one broken streak, while Manoj started small, treated the missed week as information, moved sessions to mornings and set a rule never to miss twice.
What was Jeevan feeling after the streak broke?
Like a failure, which made him give up completely.
What could Jeevan try instead?
Jeevan could start with a small daily walk and treat a missed day as something to learn from.

Uma said, "Can I play too?"
How did Salma's way of getting Aman to play differ from Charu's way with Meera, and what happened?
Salma offered the first turn on her bicycle in exchange for tag, and Aman joined in, while Charu demanded that Meera play her game or lose her as a friend, and Meera walked away.
What was Charu feeling when she stood alone in the sand?
Sad and left out, though she probably did not understand why Meera left.
What could Charu try next time?

How did Swati's way of asking for food differ from Varun's first attempts, and what did each get?
Swati handed her mother the empty bowl and got more food at once, while Varun tried the cupboard, the fridge and pointing, and got a banana rather than the biscuit he wanted.
What was Varun feeling when he shoved the banana away?
Disappointed and frustrated, because he wanted a biscuit and not a banana.
How could Varun's father help?

What did Arjun tick off each night?

What was Leela feeling by the second week?
She felt exhausted and probably discouraged, since the routine she copied did not fit her and she gave up.
What could Leela do to start again?

Then Anirban shoved baby Deepak off the play mat, and Deepak wailed. Ritu lifted Deepak, took Anirban's hand gently and said, "You're cross with me. But pushing is not okay."

Seven years later, the maths teacher called Anirban's answer silly in front of everyone, and the class laughed. Anirban said nothing all day and stared at the desk. At home the front door banged, the school bag skidded across the floor, and when the family dog trotted up wagging, Anirban snapped, "Go away!" Ritu saw the bag lying in the hallway and sat down nearby without a word. Deepak, now eight, quietly left a biscuit on the arm of the sofa. After a while Anirban muttered, "Everybody laughed at me," and the words came out in a rush.

Where did the school bag skid when Anirban came home?
The school bag skidded across the floor.
What is similar in what Anirban does at two and at nine, and what is different?

Both times anger from being told off or laughed at lands on someone safer than the person who caused it: baby Deepak at two, the door, the bag and the dog at nine. At nine the feeling eventually turns into words about school.
What was Anirban feeling when the front door banged?
Anirban was still burning with embarrassment and anger from the class laughing, and home felt like the first safe place to let it out.
How could Ritu help Anirban handle the next hard school day?
Ritu could stay calm, name the feeling, offer a safe way to let it out such as a walk or drawing, and later help Anirban plan how to speak to the teacher.

At ten, Shankar stood by the lab sink while Imran, an older student, pushed a cracked beaker into Shankar's hands. "Shove it in your bag. If anyone asks, you never saw it." Shankar's stomach dropped as if in a lift, but Imran was in Class Eight and everyone knew him. The beaker went into the bag. By lunch the bag felt as heavy as a stone, and Shankar told the class teacher everything in a small voice. The teacher said, "Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault," took the beaker and spoke to the older students that same afternoon.

At fifteen, on the football field, Coach Mahima called Shankar aside after the whistle. "The ball never crossed the line. Tell the referee you touched it last." Shankar respected Mahima, who drove the team to every match, and Shankar's mouth went dry. Shankar walked towards the referee on legs that felt borrowed and managed only, "I'm not sure." That night Shankar told Papa, who phoned the school's sports teacher the same evening and stayed close through the call.

What did Imran tell Shankar to do with the cracked beaker?
Imran told Shankar, "Shove it in your bag. If anyone asks, you never saw it."
How was the pressure on Shankar at fifteen different from the pressure at ten?

At ten it came from an older student whom Shankar could tell on; at fifteen it came from a coach Shankar respected and depended on, so refusing felt almost unthinkable. In both cases Shankar felt the request was wrong and told a trusted adult the same day.
What was Shankar feeling when Coach Mahima asked for the lie about the ball?
Shankar felt torn, with respect for the coach mixed with fear, and a dry-mouthed sense that the request was wrong.
What should the sports teacher do after Papa's call?
The sports teacher should listen to Shankar, say it is not Shankar's fault and pass the concern to the right person in the school that day.

When Sumit was two, he waved at the toy train on the shelf and shouted, "Go!" Sudha's phone rang, the train stayed put, and he waved harder, looking at his mother with wide, puzzled eyes. When she crossed the room and nudged the train, Sumit clapped. His wave had done it.

At five, Sumit would not sleep until Sudha checked under the bed for monsters and he had said the words he invented for keeping them away, "Sooty-sooty, shoo." He left a tooth under the pillow for the tooth fairy and woke at dawn to find a coin. He was sure both worked.

At ten, on the morning of the maths test, Sumit put on his lucky blue shirt, stepped over every crack in the pavement and tapped the school gate twice. Jasleen, a classmate, laughed. "That does nothing, you know." "I know," said Sumit, and tapped the gate a third time anyway.

What did Sumit leave under the pillow?
Sumit left a tooth under the pillow for the tooth fairy.
How does Sumit's belief in magic change between age two and age ten?

At two he thinks his wave moves the train, at five he trusts protection words and the tooth fairy completely, and at ten he knows the lucky shirt and gate tapping are not logical but still uses them. The belief loosens, yet the comfort stays.
What was Sumit feeling when he tapped the gate a third time after Jasleen laughed?
Sumit was anxious about the test, and although he knows the ritual is not logical, tapping still makes him feel safer.
How could Sudha respond to the monster checks at bedtime?
Sudha could check calmly and accept the protection words as a comfort, without laughing, and let Sumit grow out of them at his own pace. 🙂

At two, Harish flung a spoon to the floor and howled, face crimson, until Rekha, Harish's mother, shook a rattling tin of buttons. Inside a minute the howl turned into a giggle and the spoon was forgotten. The feeling came on like a storm and left as quickly. Rekha knew that crying which would not settle even with cuddles and a new distraction was worth mentioning to the doctor, but this was not that.

At five, Harish tripped on the playground mat, barely a scrape, and dropped flat with a long, theatrical wail, one eye checking who was watching. Uma, the class teacher, walked over unhurried, knelt and said in an even voice, "That looked like a surprise. Show me where it hurts." Harish sniffed, pointed to a knee with no mark on it and, after a moment, said, "Little bit." Uma smiled. "A little bump, then. Shall we get back to the game?" And Harish did, hopping the first few steps for show.

What did Rekha shake to stop Harish's howling?
Rekha shook a rattling tin of buttons.
How do Harish's outbursts at two and at five differ, and what did each adult's response teach?

At two the howl came on and went within a minute once a distraction appeared; at five the wail was theatrical over a tiny bump, with an eye on the audience. Rekha's distraction let the feeling pass, while Uma's calm, even reply gave the bump its proper size.
What might Harish have been feeling when checking who was watching mid-wail?
Harish probably wanted attention and comfort, and the feeling of surprise had grown much bigger than the bump.
Why did Uma's response work?
Uma stayed calm and unhurried and asked to be shown the spot, so the big display got a small, fitting reply instead of a big reaction.

At twenty, Bhupen reached the night concert early and, before the first song, counted three gates: the main one, a side gate and a narrow one by the water tank. When the crowd surged forward after the last song and people began shouting, Bhupen raised both arms in front of the chest, walked with the flow towards the side gate instead of fighting back to the meeting spot, and told Wasim, "Stay next to me. Slow steps." Outside, they were shaken but fine.

Five years later, a rant Vaibhav wrote about a local bus service travelled far beyond his friends, and strangers piled onto his posts with insults. Bhupen wrote no public defence. Instead came a private message: "Saw the comments. Are you okay? Come over and leave the phone in my bag for a bit." Vaibhav replied near midnight. Together they muted the thread, and Bhupen reported the abusive accounts, sitting beside Vaibhav until his hands stopped shaking. In the morning Bhupen brought hot samosas and did not mention the comments unless Vaibhav did.

How many gates did Bhupen count before the first song?
Bhupen counted three gates: the main one, a side gate and a narrow one by the water tank.
What do Bhupen's actions in the concert crowd and in the online pile-on have in common, and how do they differ?

In both, Bhupen stays calm and steady instead of pushing against the storm: at the concert by planning an exit and moving with the flow, online by reaching Vaibhav privately, helping him stop reading the comments and reporting the abuse. The first protects people in a physical crowd, the second protects a person hurt by an online one.
What might Vaibhav have been feeling when he replied to Bhupen near midnight?
Vaibhav was probably hurt, exposed and anxious about the insults, and relieved that someone reached out quietly.
What else could Bhupen do for Vaibhav in the following days?
Bhupen could keep checking in, help with further reports rather than arguing in public, and encourage Vaibhav to talk to someone trusted if the distress lingers.

What did Kalyani grab at age two?
Kalyani grabbed the red cup with a loud "Mine!"

How might Kalyani have felt when Naveen deleted the photo?

Gautam's smile shrank for a moment, then came back: nobody had pushed Gautam into the group. Gautam had picked it, and Arohi bumped an elbow in the next count as the music started again.

What did Gautam do when the juice ran out at age two?
Gautam stamped both feet when the juice ran out.
How does Gautam's body carry feeling at two, ten and sixteen?

At two bouncing, stamping and running show joy and anger before words; at ten pacing and a bouncing knee show nerves and need for movement; at sixteen dancing in a group shows joy and belonging. The movement stays, but its meaning and use grow.
What was Gautam feeling while pacing the corridor before the science test?
Gautam was nervous, with too much energy to sit still before the test.
What helped Gautam settle before the test, and why?
The teacher's movement break, carrying the register, let the nervous energy out so sitting still became easier. 👍

At two, Uday waved at the milkman from behind Anjali's legs, then hid in the folds of her kurta when a neighbour leaned in to say hello. Anjali, Uday's mother, only said, "Bye-bye can wait until you're ready." That evening Uday waved at the moon from the balcony and babbled, "Hello!"

At nine, a new girl called Urmila stood at the classroom door clutching her bag. Uday, usually the quiet one, moved along the bench, split a laddoo in half and pointed out the water tap and the library. "You can sit with us," Uday said, smiling shyly.

What did Uday do when a neighbour leaned in to say hello at age two?
Uday hid in the folds of Anjali's kurta.
How does Uday's way of greeting people change across the three ages?

At two Uday waved and babbled "Hello!" when ready, without being forced; at nine Uday moved along the bench, split a laddoo and pointed out the water tap for the new girl; at twenty Uday stated a name, a course and an interest in the interview room. Each greeting fits the age and builds a link.
What might Uday have been feeling while moving along the bench for Urmila?
Uday was probably feeling shy but kind, wanting Urmila to feel welcome in an unfamiliar room. 😊
What could an adult do to help a shy toddler like Uday with greetings?
An adult can let the toddler greet in their own time, as Anjali did, and welcome a wave from a distance instead of forcing a hello.

By the fourth day the name followed Manoj from the gate to the canteen, the laughter came from a wider circle, and Manoj's grin looked stuck on. Madhuri, nearby, noticed that the eyes dropped each time and that no one was laughing with Manoj any more. At lunch Madhuri went to the class teacher. The teacher spoke to the group that afternoon and checked in with Manoj the next morning.

Manoj rang Madhuri, now a close friend. "Ask what's behind it," Madhuri said. "And watch whether your choices get respected, or whether you feel afraid to say no. What nickname did the back-bench friends call out to Manoj?
They called out, "Bald eagle!"
How do the teasing at ten and the ultimatum at twenty each need a closer look to tell whether something is fine or harmful?

At ten a joke turned into mocking as it repeated, spread to a wider circle and Manoj stopped laughing, so watching the target's face and the pattern mattered. At twenty "quit or I'm done" could be a real need or pressure, so Manoj asked what was behind it and whether choices were respected.
What was Manoj feeling on the fourth day of the nickname?
Manoj felt hurt and cornered, and the stuck grin covered it.
What did Manoj do after the ultimatum that helped?
Manoj talked to a trusted friend, then asked Jaya what was really wrong, which led to a plan that respected both people's needs.

How do Vijay's worries at nine and at fifteen resemble each other, and how did help differ?

What was Vijay feeling when the desk stayed tidy and the books unopened?
Vijay was anxious and overwhelmed, feeling that worrying was a kind of responsibility even though it replaced studying.

At ten, Francis received a thick envelope of Diwali money from relatives and spent all of it in one afternoon on sweets and a toy. The next week, with his own pocket money down to ten rupees, he refused to spend even that on a pencil box. Payal, his older sister, noticed. "It's all just money, you know." Francis shrugged. "Gift money doesn't count."

At sixteen, he won a quiz voucher and used it up in a day on games, yet he guarded the cash he earned running errands for the neighbours, counting it twice before closing the tin.

At twenty, Francis got a bonus from his campus job and bought a pair of earbuds without a second thought. Walking home the same evening, he skipped the bus to save a couple of rupees. Seema, a flatmate, watched him arrive footsore. "You just spent the bonus on earbuds, and now you're walking to save a bus fare?" Francis laughed. "The bonus was extra."

What did Francis spend the Diwali money on?
Francis spent all of it in one afternoon on sweets and a toy.
What do the three stages show about how Francis treats money from different sources?

At ten gift money counted as free to spend while pocket money felt precious; at sixteen a quiz voucher went in a day while earned cash was guarded; at twenty a bonus was spent easily while a small bus fare was saved. Francis's mind sorts the same rupees into separate pots by where they came from.
What might Francis have been feeling when he said, "Gift money doesn't count"?
Francis probably felt carefree and a little defensive, sure the gift belonged to a different category from his own money.
How could Payal help her brother notice how he sorts money, without lecturing?
Payal could kindly point out that a rupee from a gift and a rupee from pocket money buy the same things, and ask Francis how he decides which feels spendable.

Three years later, while the family planned a cousin's wedding, a list of gifts began to circulate. Bidisha, a cousin, said calmly, "I'd rather we drop this list and ask what the couple needs." Nobody spoke. Then Thomas, an uncle, said, "She's right. We did this once and regretted it." Two aunts nodded. The list was shelved slowly, over three visits, not in one evening, and no one raised a voice.

What did Naveen tell his parents he would not take?
Naveen said, "I will not take dowry in any form."
How are Naveen's stand at twenty-two and Bidisha's at the wedding planning similar and different?

Naveen told his parents he would not take dowry before any date was fixed, and Bidisha said calmly that she would rather drop the gift list while the family planned the wedding. Both spoke early and calmly, Naveen as the groom and Bidisha as a cousin, and Thomas and two aunts backed her, so one clear voice made others braver.
What was Naveen's mother probably feeling when she told him she was relieved?
She was probably feeling quiet relief and pride that her son had said aloud what she may not have felt able to say.
What could Bidisha do next after the list was shelved?
Bidisha could thank the elders who backed her and keep the talk about what the couple needs, staying patient since change is slower than anger.

At fifteen, he sat in an evening coaching class for chemistry that he hated, and could not follow. His parents had paid the fees for two years and the fees for the third were due. "If I leave now, all that money is wasted," he said, and he went again, tired. His marks did not improve, and his weekends disappeared. At twenty, Yusuf was in the second year of a commerce degree that no longer fit him. He was drawn to marine biology, but leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted. His friend Hansa asked one afternoon, "If you were starting today, knowing what you know, would you choose this?" He was quiet a long time. "No," he said, and looked out at the rain, stunned to hear it aloud.

What food did Yusuf make himself finish at nine?
He made himself finish the bitter gourd.
What is the same about Yusuf's reasons for continuing at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine he kept eating and playing because of the money and hour already spent, at fifteen he stayed in the coaching class because of the fees paid, and at twenty he stayed in the degree because leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted. Each time past effort decided what he did next.
What was Yusuf feeling when he said no to Hansa's question?
He felt stunned and quietly relieved to say it aloud, after years of pushing on.
What could Yusuf do next to choose his future rather than his past?
He could learn what marine biology courses need, talk to Hansa or a counsellor, and decide by asking what he wants from now on.

She deleted her comment.
How does Rajni's part in a crowd at ten, fifteen and twenty share a pattern?

At ten she pushed with the others without deciding to, at fifteen she added a comment because everyone had, and at twenty she chanted louder than she would alone and was carried by the surge. What was Rajni feeling when she saw the classmate's face at her desk?
She felt ashamed and guilty, as her sinking stomach shows, realising the target had seen every word.
What could Rajni do next time she notices herself swept along in a crowd?
She could pause and ask herself whether she would do it alone, and step out to the side with a friend if things turn unsafe.

On the seventh day, a pale green loop pushed up through the soil. "I did that," Farhan whispered, and he ran to show everyone. At fifteen, his family moved cities after his father's job ended, and money was tight and tempers short. Farhan could not stop the arguments. What did Farhan plant with his grandfather?
He planted a bean seed.
How does Farhan's sense of influence at nine connect to what he does at fifteen?

At nine planting the seed and fixing the truck showed him that his actions changed things, and at fifteen he used that belief to list what was his to change, like studying and asking for help, and what was not, like his father's job. Acting on the first list gave him power in a hard time.
What was Farhan feeling when he saw the pale green loop push up through the soil?
He felt proud and amazed, because it showed him that his effort had made something happen.
What could Farhan do if he feels helpless again about things outside his control?
He could go back to his list, choose one small step from it, and keep talking to Simran about how he feels.

At sixteen, Kalyani's friend Santosh pointed at his cousin's motorbike. "Come on, three of us fit. It's only ten minutes." Kalyani shook her head. "No, I'm taking the bus. Want to get tea after?" He rolled his eyes. "My mother tracks my location anyway," she added, which was partly true, and they laughed. But by the next week he was asking again, and again, and calling her boring. Kalyani felt her resolve wobble. She told her aunt Rukmini, who said, "Good friends accept a no. Would you like me to talk with him, or would you rather do it yourself?" Kalyani chose to talk to him alone. Nine years later, Kalyani and Santosh were partners in a small bakery. He wanted to buy a costly oven at once, while she wanted to wait a year. Voices rose. Then she said, "We both want the shop to last. Let's rent an oven for three months and see. If it works, we buy, and I'll happily agree that you were right about needing one." Santosh let out a laugh. "Three months. Deal."

What did Kalyani suggest to Santosh instead of the motorbike?
She said she was taking the bus and asked if he wanted tea afterwards.
How is Kalyani's way of handling disagreement at sixteen linked to her way at twenty-five?

At sixteen she shook her head, said she was taking the bus, asked about tea and told her aunt Rukmini when Santosh kept asking. At twenty-five, when voices rose over the oven, she said they both wanted the shop to last and offered to rent an oven for three months and see.
What was Kalyani feeling when Santosh kept asking again and calling her boring?
She felt pressured and unsure of herself, and her resolve wobbled.
What could Kalyani do if Santosh keeps pressuring her about risky things?

What did Sunaina ask her grandmother about the light?
She asked why Lakshmi swings the light.
How does Sunaina's reading of ritual differ at five and at twenty?

At five she copied her grandmother's clapping and asked why the light is swung, learning that actions mark special moments. At twenty she read the wedding procession of drummers, dancers and a groom on a horse as joy, and asked Aditi what the song meant before joining.
What was Sunaina feeling when she asked about the song at the procession?
She felt respectful and a little unsure, wanting to join without doing anything wrong.

What did Baljeet fold for his grandfather's birthday?
He folded a paper boat.
How do the responses to Baljeet's work matter at two, ten and twenty?

What was Baljeet feeling when Joseph called the film heartbreaking?
He felt surprised and a bit puzzled, because he had meant viewers to feel calm.
What could Baljeet do to learn how his film comes across?

What did Devika build on the holiday afternoon?
She built a fort.
How do Devika's flat feelings at nine, twenty and twenty-five relate to one another?

What was Devika feeling when she asked why she felt nothing after getting what she wanted?
She felt hollow and confused, missing the sense of direction her goal had given her.
What could Devika try to bring some direction back into her routine?
She could pick a small project she cares about, like a course or a new hobby, and set aside a regular hour for it instead of aimless videos.

Baby Pema was fourteen months old when her grandfather Bhupen leaned over her cot each morning. Her whole face opened: mouth wide, eyes crinkled, both fists waving. Bhupen smiled back just as widely and said, "There you are!" She squealed, and the two of them went on trading looks until the kettle whistled.

Seven years later Pema stood at the door of a new school, holding her bag strap with both hands. The teacher, Siddharth, said, "Good morning, Pema, welcome." Her lips pressed together into a small, neat smile, and her eyes dropped to her shoes.

Siddharth did not say, "Come on, give me a big smile." He nodded, pointed at a desk by the window and said, "That one is yours whenever you are ready to sit." Pema let out a breath, walked over and unzipped her bag. By lunch she had shown a classmate her pencil case, and her smile had grown, though only by a little.

Who leaned over Pema's cot each morning when she was fourteen months old?
Her grandfather Bhupen leaned over her cot each morning.
How does Pema's smile at fourteen months differ from her smile at seven years, and what changed in how the adult answered?

As a baby she gave a wide, open smile that Bhupen matched, building a back-and-forth of attention; at school she gave a small closed smile of shyness, and Siddharth gave her time instead of asking for more.
What was Pema likely feeling as she stood at the new classroom door?
Pema was probably shy and unsure, gripping her bag strap and looking at her shoes, yet polite enough to smile a little.
What did Siddharth do that helped Pema settle in?
Siddharth greeted her warmly, did not push her for a bigger smile, and pointed out her desk so she could sit when ready.

At twenty, as an intern, she sent her manager Swati a long email that began with her weekend and wandered through three projects. The request for approval sat in the last line. Swati replied in ten minutes: "Happy to sign off. Next time, put what you need from me at the top." Pallavi rewrote her template that evening, putting the question in the first sentence and the details underneath.

What did Pallavi write in Class Four?
She wrote, "He went there and it was bad, so they left."
What is different about the writing trouble at nine, fifteen and twenty, and what stays the same?

At nine Pallavi left out steps, at fifteen she stretched sentences with long words, and at twenty she buried the request in a long email; each time the reader struggled, and clear writing put the reader first.
What might Pallavi be feeling when Vidya asks who and where?
Pallavi is puzzled, since the story is so clear in her head that she cannot see what is missing for the reader.
What could Pallavi do before sending her next email?
She could open with the request for Swati, then add the details below, since the purpose should be visible in the first lines.

Then he tripped, burst into tears and rubbed his eyes. She lifted him, dimmed the lights and said, "You are so tired, aren't you?" He was asleep in ten minutes.

At nine, Jomon slumped at his desk with his chin on his arm, yawning through the first period and snapping at a friend. His teacher did not send him out. They asked quietly after class, "You seem worn out. How is bedtime going, and how is the noise at home?" Jomon said the new baby next door cried half the night.

At twenty-five, Jomon made three small errors in a report and stopped laughing at meetings. His colleague Joseph found him alone at the kitchenette one afternoon. "You've seemed drained lately. Anything I can take off your plate?" Jomon let out a shaky breath.

What did Sonali do after Jomon tripped and burst into tears?
She lifted him, dimmed the lights and told him he was so tired.
What do the three scenes show about how adults and colleagues can read tiredness in Jomon?

At two a wild burst is a sign that a nap is overdue, at nine slumping and a short temper lead a teacher to ask about bedtime, and at twenty-five small mistakes lead Joseph to check in kindly, so each observer looks past the behaviour to the tiredness.
How was Jomon probably feeling as he slumped at his desk at nine?
Jomon was worn out and irritable, low on sleep because of the crying baby next door, which shortened his temper.
What could a colleague do besides criticising the errors?
A colleague can check in privately, as Joseph did, and ask what could be taken off the plate, since kindness helps more than gossip.

Five-year-old Pallavi crept up to her Nana Kamal as he read the newspaper with a flat, still face. "Are you angry at me?" she whispered. Kamal lowered the paper. "No, beta, I'm only thinking about the crossword. My face gets serious when I think." Pallavi let out a breath and climbed onto his lap.

At fifteen, Pallavi's friend Reena got a phone call in the corridor about her grandmother's fall. Reena's face turned rigid, eyes fixed, mouth closed. She did not cry or speak. Pallavi did not say, "Why don't you say something?" She sat beside her on the stairs, passed her water and waited. After a long time Reena said, "I can't feel anything yet."

At twenty-four, Pallavi noticed her colleague Tarun sitting with a blank expression through meeting after meeting for weeks. She did not decide that he was bored. After work she said, "You've seemed drained. Do you want me to take the client call tomorrow?" Tarun's shoulders dropped.

What did Nana Kamal say his serious face meant?
Kamal said he was only thinking about the crossword and that his face gets serious when he thinks.
What do the three scenes have in common about reading a still face?

At five a flat, still face on Kamal means only thinking; at fifteen Reena's rigid face is shock after the call about her grandmother's fall; at twenty-four Tarun's blank expression means he is drained, not bored. Pallavi answers with a question or quiet help, not judgement.
What might Reena be feeling on the stairs after the phone call?
Reena is probably in shock and fear about her grandmother, feeling numb, which is why her face is frozen.
What did Pallavi do for Tarun that suited his blank face?
She avoided judging his attitude, asked privately in kind words how he was, and offered practical help by taking the client call.

At two, Payal held out her wooden giraffe to her uncle after he handed her a picture book, then hugged his knee. Her mother whispered, "Say thank you," and Payal chirped it back, beaming at the book more than at the words.

At fifteen, she sent hearts and a row of clapping emojis under her friend Sangeeta's post about the school play, and then paused. It felt a bit easy. She typed a separate message: "The way you held the last note when your voice shook made me cry. You did that so well." Sangeeta replied in seconds: "You have no idea how much I needed that. 🙂"

At twenty-five, in a team meeting, Payal said, "Before I present the numbers, Binita found the error in our first draft last Thursday and rebuilt the whole sheet over the weekend. Without her, this would have been wrong." Binita looked up, surprised, and smiled.

What did Payal hand over to her uncle at two?
Payal handed her uncle her wooden giraffe.
How does Payal's way of showing appreciation develop from two to fifteen to twenty-five?

At two she gives a toy and a hug and repeats a prompted thank you, at fifteen she moves from quick hearts to a specific personal message, and at twenty-five she gives specific, public credit for Binita's real work in a meeting.
What was Sangeeta feeling when she replied that Payal had no idea how much she needed the message?
Sangeeta was moved and grateful, feeling that the specific message meant more than a row of reactions.
Why did Payal's credit for Binita work well?
It was specific, timely and public, naming what Binita did and when, so Binita felt recognised and the team saw the real contribution.

At nine, Harish noticed something: every day he wore his red shirt, his cricket team won. His sister Minakshi laughed when he refused to wash it before the final. "The shirt is why we win," he said, with a straight face. She asked, "What about the day we won when you wore blue?" Harish frowned. He hadn't thought of that.

At fifteen, he saw that students who joined tuition classes scored more in the unit tests, and told his father he needed tuition. His classmate Yamini said, "The ones who go to tuition also do their homework early and have quiet study rooms. Maybe tuition isn't the only reason."

At twenty, in the college canteen, he read a headline claiming that people who drink coffee tend to live longer, and started buying a large cup every morning. Yamini looked at the article with him. "Does it say coffee causes it? Maybe healthier, richer people just drink more of it. Or people who are already ill drink less." Harish pushed the cup aside and kept reading.

What colour was the shirt Harish thought brought his team luck?
The shirt was red.
What thinking mistake does Harish make at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine Harish links the red shirt to wins, at fifteen tuition to higher scores and at twenty coffee to a longer life, each time deciding that one thing causes the other without asking what else might explain both.
What was Harish feeling when Minakshi asked about the day they won in blue?
Harish was puzzled and a little caught out, because he had not thought of that day, and he frowned.
What could Harish ask himself the next time a headline links two things?
He could ask whether something else, such as health or money, might explain both, or whether the link runs the other way, as Yamini suggested.

In Class Five, Hafsa watched her teacher Nirmala's face after every question. When Nirmala's eyebrows rose at "eleven", Hafsa quickly changed it to "twelve", then glanced back to check. She no longer knew which answer she believed. She simply wanted the smile that came when she was right.

At fifteen, Hafsa stood on the wall of the school water tank after a dare, with a ring of classmates cheering and phones raised. Her legs shook. She felt proud and sick at once. Sachin, the sports coach, saw it from the courtyard and walked over fast, staying calm. "Come down slowly, I'm right here," he said, and steadied her hand. Later he sat with her and asked, "What were you proving, and to whom?"

Hafsa was quiet a long while. The next week, when a friend copied her homework, she said no, and it was harder than the wall had ever been. Her voice shook, but it was her own.

Where did Hafsa stand after the dare at fifteen?
Hafsa stood on the wall of the school water tank.
How do Hafsa's behaviour in Class Five and on the tank wall link approval with courage?

In Class Five she changes her answers to win the teacher's smile, and on the wall she risks a fall for the cheering crowd, so both come from needing approval; saying no to her friend later serves her own value, which is what real courage does.
What was Hafsa probably feeling on the wall, with the crowd cheering and her legs shaking?
Hafsa felt proud and frightened at once, wanting the crowd's approval while sick with fear of falling.
What did Sachin do that helped Hafsa?
Sachin stayed calm, told her to come down slowly, steadied her hand, and later asked what she was proving and to whom.

Weeks later he was still slow, and tired. Mahima sat beside him. "Ask me anything. I asked ten questions a day in my first month." Tenzin, the lead, nodded from across the room.

Who noticed Suraj rereading the same file for an hour?
His colleague Mahima noticed him rereading the same file for an hour.
How are Suraj's thoughts in his first semester and at his first job linked?

At the institute Suraj felt like a fraud who would be found out, and at work the same feeling makes him overwork and avoid asking questions, so the imposter feeling shows up as hiding gaps, which slows his learning.
What was Suraj feeling when Mahima asked whether he was stuck?
Suraj felt afraid of being exposed, so he denied it and mumbled that he was just checking.
What could Suraj try next?
He could accept Mahima's offer and ask a question each day, since asking for help exposes less than long hours of hidden struggling.

At nine, Jasleen read aloud slowly, stumbling over long words, and her classmates waited. That evening she pushed her book away. "I'm dumb," she said. "I can't read." The next day she stopped raising her hand at all. Her father Ojas sat beside her and asked, "Which words tripped you?" There were only four, and they practised them until bedtime. The label "dumb" shrank to four hard words.

At fifteen, Jasleen was going to interview for a summer job at the library. Her heart hammered, her hands felt cold and she couldn't sit still. "I'm terrified," she told her friend Rafiq. He tilted his head. "You've got the same racing heart as before your trip to the hills. That was excitement." She thought about it, took a breath and said aloud, "I'm excited. I'm nervous, but I'm ready."

Her heart was still racing as she walked into the interview, but now it had a different name.

How many words tripped Jasleen when she read aloud at nine?
Only four words tripped her.
How do the names Jasleen gives herself at nine and at fifteen show the effect of labels?

At nine the label "dumb" makes her stop trying, until Ojas turns it into four hard words she can practise; at fifteen she renames a racing heart from terrified to excited and nervous but ready, so the label shapes what she does next.
What was Jasleen feeling when she told Rafiq she was terrified?
Jasleen was anxious and afraid, with her heart hammering and her hands cold, although the same body signals could also mean excitement.
What did Ojas do that helped Jasleen at nine?
He asked which words tripped her and practised the four hard ones with her, replacing a vague label with a skill that could be practised.

What was Kunal probably feeling as he sharpened the pencils twice at nine?
Kunal was anxious about the hard division and used easy jobs to escape the fear for a while, though his stomach stayed tight.
