Harsha sat quietly beside him, said he was there, and shrank the task to just the first sum, so Kunal could start.

His father Yogesh never asked about the game they had played on Sunday or the lunch he had shared. He asked only, "What did you score?" and then, "Why not full marks?" Kishore began to hide any paper with a red cross, and learned to say, "It went well."

His mother Vasudha noticed him rubbing a hole into his notebook while erasing a tiny wrong figure. She felt proud of how hard he tried and worried that he was so afraid of mistakes. That evening she said, "Yesterday I burned the dal and forgot to buy tea. Everybody slips, and ordinary work is enough, you know." She did not tell him to lower his standards. Kishore looked at the notebook and laughed a little, a real laugh for the first time that week.

What was the missing mark that mattered to Kishore on his 92 test?
The missing eight mattered most to him.
How do Yogesh's questions and Vasudha's evening talk show different parental responses to the same child?

Yogesh responds only to marks, which makes Kishore feel loved for performance and hide his mistakes, while Vasudha, torn between pride and worry, shares her own mistakes and says everybody slips and ordinary work is enough, without shaming his high standards.
What was Vasudha feeling when she saw the hole in Kishore's notebook?
Vasudha felt proud of his effort and worried about his fear of mistakes, torn between the two.
What could Yogesh ask instead of "What did you score?"
He could ask about the day, the game and what Kishore enjoyed or learned, so that love does not seem to depend on marks.

Every version looked flawed to him: the second heading was clumsy, the third source felt weak. Other students were already drafting. Reading one more article seemed safer than writing a single paragraph that could be marked down.

On the deadline's eve Gautam looked at the tidy, untouched document and thought of the atlas. He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence anyway, though his stomach was tight.

How many times did Gautam redraw the outline?
He redrew the outline eleven times.
How is the way Gautam hid papers at nine linked to his endless preparation at twenty-one?

At nine Gautam learns that love and approval follow marks, so he hides mistakes; at twenty-one the same fear of a marked-down page keeps him researching and redrawing the outline rather than starting, which is perfectionism as paralysis.
What was Gautam probably feeling as he told his roommate the outline was not ready to show anyone?
Gautam was afraid of being judged, so preparing felt safer than exposing a rough draft.
What small step did Gautam take on the eve of the deadline, and why does it matter?
He opened a blank page and typed a rough sentence, which breaks the cycle of preparing because a rough start is easier than a perfect one.

Ten minutes into a rainy Sunday, five-year-old Tejas flopped on the sofa. "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the tablet?" His father Vikas looked up from the newspaper. He did not hand over the tablet, and he did not offer a list of ideas. He put a large cardboard box, a roll of tape and a marker on the floor. "Here," he said, and went back to reading. Tejas sighed and complained for a minute. Then he cut a hole in the side and announced, "It's a bus."

At ten, in the long heat of a summer afternoon with no screens, Tejas draped bedsheets over two chairs and the bookcase. He built a fort with a secret entrance, drew a map of his kingdom and invented a card game with his cousin Saurabh that filled hours. When his father called for tea, Tejas said, "Five more minutes." He had not looked at the clock once.

What did Vikas put on the floor when Tejas said he was bored?
Vikas put down a large cardboard box, a roll of tape and a marker.
How does Tejas's boredom at five lead to his afternoon at ten?

At five he feels the discomfort of boredom and asks for a screen, but simple materials and time turn it into a bus; by ten the same boredom, left alone, becomes a fort, a map and a card game, showing that tolerated boredom grows self-directed interest.
What was Tejas feeling when he flopped on the sofa and asked for the tablet?
Tejas felt restless and uncomfortable, wanting the easy relief of a screen.
What did Vikas do that helped Tejas at five?
Vikas gave simple materials without solving the boredom for Tejas, so the boy could invent something himself.

At five, Manjula clapped a hand over her mouth and shrieked with giggles whenever her father Arnab made his moustache wiggle and called the cat "Mister Cow." She tried the wrong words herself: "Papa, the spoon is a shoe!" They laughed until the tea went cold, leaning into each other.

What word did Manjula trip over when reading aloud at nine?
Manjula tripped over the word "temperature".
How does the humour Manjula uses at five differ from the humour she uses at nine?

At five Manjula giggles with Arnab over wrong words and funny faces; at nine she crosses her eyes and says "Tempra-tricycle" so the class roars after she trips, then goes quiet at her desk. The first is shared play, the second is a joke that keeps control of the moment and hides worry.
What was Manjula probably feeling when she tore at the edge of her notebook after class?
Manjula was embarrassed and worried underneath the jokes, and her torn notebook edge showed the nervousness she had covered with clowning.
What did Farida do that helped Manjula?
Farida praised the funny rescue, named that reading aloud can feel scary, and offered to practise the hard words together.

On Thursday, Dhruv told his mother Disha that his science project would take ten minutes and he would begin after dinner on Friday. "It's only a chart," he said. On Friday night he found he had to cut out pictures, look up three facts and colour the border. At half past nine he was still gluing, and the chart had gone crooked.

Earlier that week, Dhruv had promised his father Uday, "I'll draw the mango in five minutes, then we can go to the park." Uday looked at the clock. An hour later Dhruv was still shading the leaves, absorbed and surprised. "Is it evening already?" he asked. He had not been trying to fool anyone. He truly thought five minutes was enough.

On Saturday, Uday sat with him and wrote next to each task how long the last one had taken. Dhruv stared at the list and said, "Oh. It's not ten minutes, it's more like an hour."

How long did Dhruv say his science project would take?
Dhruv said the project would take ten minutes.
What do the science chart and the mango drawing have in common?

In both Dhruv gives a short time, ten minutes for the chart and five for the mango, and then finds it takes far longer, because he pictures the ideal path and has little sense of how long things take, so his promises are sincere but unreliable.
What was Dhruv feeling when he asked whether it was evening already?
Dhruv felt surprised and absorbed, honestly unaware that an hour had gone.
What could Uday do to help Dhruv plan time better?
Uday could do what he did, writing down how long each task really took, so Dhruv can compare guesses with real times.

How are the delay at sixteen and the all-night sprint at twenty connected?

What was Devika probably feeling as she opened and closed the file every evening at sixteen?
Devika was afraid of doing badly, so she protected her self-image by not starting.

What did Zeenat pretend to do when she stumbled on the word eruption?

How is Zeenat's joke in class at nine like the memes she posts at fifteen?
